#2511. Austin Reaves steps up in Luka Doncic's absence to lead Lakers over Pistons

The Lakers' star guard banked in a fadeaway three-pointer. He nailed a clutch step-back with 44.5 seconds left. He trash-talked with fans.

Reaves embodied Doncic in almost every way Sunday, leading the Lakers to a 121-116 win over the Detroit Pistons as Doncic sat out with low back tightness. The Lakers replaced the guard averaging a league-high 40.1 points with Reaves' season-high 43 points, four assists and five rebounds.

The Lakers (9-2) needed every bit of Reaves' magic. Their 26-point second-quarter lead nearly evaporated under an avalanche of second-half turnovers and 55 combined points from Detroit bench guards Daniss Jenkins and Kevin Huerter.

Fresh off a max contract extension, Reaves has had a quiet yet ruthlessly efficient start to the year in Doncic's shadow. Doncic is getting most valuable player chants each time he steps to the free throw line. Reaves, averaging 25.3 points per game on 50.8% shooting from the field and 41.3% from three, has at times looked clumsy while getting comfortable with new teammates in the minutes without Doncic.

Read more: Luka Doncic's historic run jump-starts early MVP conversation

He looked comfortable in the starring role again Sunday. Reaves hit a seemingly impossible baseline fadeaway in the first quarter, flinging the ball almost over the backboard. When two fans sitting opposite the Lakers' bench started chirping at Reaves, he bent down, put his hands on his knees during a stoppage of play and talked directly at them for several seconds.

Doncic, dressed in black pants and a gray jacket, took it all in from the sideline.

"Sometimes when they're playing together, AR kind of has to take a secondary role," said center Walker Kessler, who had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including a clutch put-back, three-point play that put the Lakers up by eight with 2:15 remaining. "But I mean, as you can see now, he's very capable. He's a heck of a playmaker, heck of a scorer and a competitor."

On the front side of a back-to-back, Doncic missed his second game of the season with low back tightness, although Lakers coach JJ Redick said he didn't anticipate it to affect Doncic significantly throughout the season.

The Slovenian superstar is averaging a league-high 40.1 points per game, but Doncic was doing more than just scoring at rates not seen since Wilt Chamberlain. His estimated on/off of 37.7 — the difference between the Lakers' net rating when he was on the court compared to off — was the second-highest in the league, following only Victor Wembanyama's 41.5. In addition to having the highest scoring average through nine games since Chamberlain, Doncic is the team's second-leading rebounder at 7.8 per game and is second with 1.7 steals.

Austin Reaves goes to the basket against Pistons guard Kevin Huerter in the second half Sunday. (Duane Burleson / Associated Press)

But the Lakers already showed they could compete without Doncic this season. They dominated the Clippers on Oct. 28 when he was sidelined, also with back tightness.

Just as they did against the Clippers, the Lakers needed contributions from everyone. Ziaire Williams hit four three-pointers and finished with 17 points. Collin Sexton, serving as the Lakers' second ball-handler, had 17 points on five-of-10 shooting.

Jarred Vanderbilt's energetic six rebounds, two assists and one block in less than six minutes during the first quarter helped lift the Lakers to a 26-point lead early in the second.

The Pistons, playing without All-NBA center Jalen Duren (hamstring), didn't get their first points from star point guard Cade Cunningham until early in the third quarter. Instead, Jenkins nearly mounted the comeback on his own.

Jenkins, a familiar Lakers foe who scored 30 points in Detroit's win over the Lakers here last year, scored 22 points of his career-high 31 in the first half, cutting the Lakers' 26-point lead to 13 by halftime. He drained a three-pointer at the buzzer that injected life into the antsy home crowd. The Lakers, who have benefited from two halftime buzzer-beating heaves from Doncic this season, know what it's like to be on the other side of that momentum swing.

Read more: Swanson: Luka Doncic can lead Lakers to a title, but only if his teammates pull their weight

Pistons fans banging inflatable thunder sticks erupted in the third quarter as Detroit ripped off an 11-0 run to close the lead to three with 1:03 remaining in the quarter. The Lakers, playing with Sexton as their primary ball-handler during the stretch, had four turnovers during the drought, including a shot clock violation after a timeout.

Reaves rested from the sideline during the slide, but Redick stayed committed to the pre-determined rotation matrix to ensure star players get their necessary breaks.

"If you start just overreacting in-game and saying 'I gotta get this guy back in, I gotta get this guy back in,' it's just chaos," Redick said. "And we're trying to create consistency for our players."

Redick called Reaves "Mr. Consistency" earlier this season. He had 13 points in the third quarter, including five straight on difficult fadeway jumpers that pushed the lead to 17 with 6:41 to go in the third. After his step-back three from the wing kissed off the glass and rattled through the rim, Reaves shrugged.

"It was 100% lucky," said Reaves, who called the daring step-back the type of ill-advised shot Doncic would attempt.

Reaves shot Doncic's shots then talked Doncic's talk. After hitting the dagger shot to put the Lakers up by eight with 44.5 seconds left, Reaves turned and waved goodbye directly to the two fans sitting courtside.

#2509. Grading every NBA lottery pick's first two weeks as impressive 2026 rookie class dazzles early

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If there's one takeaway from the first two weeks of the 2026-27 NBA season (other than the fact that there are way too many injuries), it might be this: this rookie class has the potential to be the best in league history. Maybe that's an overreaction and a case of recency bias, but the stats and film don't lie.

This group of players was heralded as one of the best freshmen classes in college basketball history. Not only did those players meet expectations, but they also went beyond them. It's hard to see a collection of talent hitting college basketball again like that for a long time.

Wizards forward AJ Dybantsa was late to the party, but the No. 1 overall pick finally made his debut last week against the Cavaliers after missing the first four games due to an ankle injury. Dybantsa scored 19 points in his first game while being on a minutes restriction.

The biggest surprise in the NBA is the Memphis Grizzlies, the only team in the association that hasn't suffered a loss. Cameron Boozer, who has seemingly won at every place he's played — whether in high school, Team USA, Duke and now the NBA — remains the favorite to win NBA Rookie of the Year over Kings guard Darius Acuff Jr. and Bulls forward Caleb Wilson.

With the first two weeks of the season in the books, it's time to assess the play of every lottery pick from the 2026 NBA Draft by handing out some early grades. Let's dive in, starting with Dybantsa.

It took exactly 16 seconds to showcase one of Dybantsa's elite skills: drawing contact at the rim. In 35 games last season at BYU, Dybantsa attempted 296 free throws, which ranked No. 1 among all college players. That's going to be a huge part of his game throughout his career because of how good he is at getting into the lane and drawing fouls. He has already attempted nine free throws in his first two games. Dybantsa is still on a minutes restriction.

AJ Dybantsa looking comfortable in his second career game 😯17 PTS | 8 REB 🔥 pic.twitter.com/px5FjLar5t

Once that restriction gets lifted, he will play even more than the 57 minutes he played during the first two games combined. The Wizards have a chance to be a sleeper play-in team in a loaded Eastern Conference this season.

Peterson's role with Utah is still being established. Something that stood out to me was Jazz coach Will Hardy benching Peterson for the final stretch against the Spurs last week, even though the game went to overtime and the team was already without Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen. There were a handful of plays in the fourth quarter where Peterson didn't make the right read on the defensive end, but the decision to bench the young rookie and only play him 26 minutes might've cost Utah a chance to steal a game at home.

Despite Peterson still trying to find a clear-cut role, he ranks fifth in his rookie class among field goals attempted (78) this season. Peterson thrives on-ball but is also very capable off the ball. That's why I really liked him as a fit with the Jazz. Peterson is going to figure it out.

Boozer is the ultimate winner. Since high school, Boozer has a 155-17 record across games in high school, at Duke and in the NBA. It should come as no surprise that he's contributing to winning at the highest level. Boozer had his first career triple-double (18/12/12) and followed it up with a career-high 27 points against Sacramento. Even when Boozer isn't playing well, he can still impact winning with his passing.

Cameron Boozer career-high 27 vs Kings:27 PTS | 9 REB | 1 BLK | 8/14 FG | 77 TS% pic.twitter.com/vRuH59q21R

He is an elite processor of the game and it's only going to get better throughout his career. The one concern I do have about Boozer is the rim finishing. Per Synergy, he is shooting 42.4% at the rim. Aside from that, Boozer has been awesome. If the Grizzlies keep winning, Boozer should be the favorite to win Rookie of the Year.

The Bulls are off to a slow start, but Wilson is not. The way he can impact both ends of the floor remains one of his strengths. Wilson is also fearless and won't back down from anybody. Two of my favorite plays so far from the NBA season came in Bulls vs. Celtics games. On the defensive end, Wilson recovered while Jayson Tatum was driving middle and rejected him at the rim with his off hand. In a game against Boston days before, Wilson had the ball at the top of the key against Paul George, jab-stepped left and dunked it while taking contact.

look at this block by Caleb Wilson on Tatum omg pic.twitter.com/1vSkEUhaOU

He is averaging 3.2 stocks (steals and blocks) per game. Another note: He is taking 7.8 (!) 3-pointers per game after taking 27 total attempts at North Carolina last season. The efficiency (29.8%) isn't there yet, but if Wilson's shooting ticks up, it changes his entire ceiling.

Wagler has been playing in a sixth man role during the first two weeks. The Clippers are trying to bring him along slowly. I'll say this: It's time to start Wagler. He has looked very comfortable even dating back to his first minutes against Sacramento. Wagler is shooting better from 3 (31.3%) than 2 (24%), but I'm not super worried about the efficiency for him or any rookie guard on the list for one reason: Rookie guards are historically inefficient.

Again, it's understandable why the Clippers want to wait to start Wagler, but it's time to put him in the starting lineup and play him even more. Wagler has shown he's capable of taking on that responsibility while running the second unit.

Similar to Wagler, Brown is coming off the bench to begin his career. He has played over 25 minutes just once this season due to the team placing him on a minutes restriction. Brown also didn't play against Indiana last weekend due to back injury management. In the game (against Boston), where Brown played over 25 minutes, he was electric in the fourth quarter. Brown scored 13 of his 17 points in the final frame, including a corner 3-pointer to send the game to overtime. Brown made a rookie mistake in overtime, attempting a layup with less than five seconds remaining, with his team up by one and the shot clock off.

After that miss, Tatum knocked down a game-winner. Brown had NBA range during his time at Louisville, and that was on display against the Celtics. It's just a matter of time before Brooklyn lifts the minutes restriction and throws him into the starting lineup.

Acuff has become the most polarizing rookie to talk about. The Kings are bad. Like, potentially the worst team in the league. However, Acuff has been the bright spot. His shotmaking is second-to-none in his class. When Acuff is hot, he can score at will. Acuff joined exclusive company earlier this week when he finished with 34 points and 14 assists against the Pelicans. The only other teenager in NBA history to post at least 30 points and 12 assists in a game, per CBS Sports research? LeBron James.

DARIUS. ACUFF. JR.Shakes his defender and drills the 3!A game-high 21 points through two quarters for the @SacramentoKings' rookie 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/hA98OwsWvL

Acuff has the ultimate green light in Sacramento. It's going to stay that way throughout his rookie season. It feels more like a matter of when, not if, Acuff scores 45+ points in a game. It might even come before the calendar flips to 2027

Flemings' best game came last week against Miami, when he finished with 23 points, five assists, five rebounds and a block/steal. Flemings' role with the Hawks this season was always going to be off the bench, so it shouldn't come as a surprise that he has scored 27 points combined in the other six games he has played in.

Flemings doesn't have to score to make an impact on the game. He was heralded as one of the best two-way players in the class, which was on display in his last game against New Orlenos when he recorded four steals. Flemings uses his speed to his advantage to get to the rim, create his own shot and change the pace. Despite taking six field goal attempts per game, Flemings has been very efficient (47.6%).

Johnson has come off the bench in his first six games under his former college coach, Dusty May. Although his numbers don't necessarily pop, Johnson is going to be a very impactful player, especially on the defensive end of the floor. He's capable of guarding 1-5, which is super valuable when/if the Mavs decide to switch everything on defense.

Burries is coming off the bench for the Bucks, which somewhat surprises me. He was awesome in summer league and should be playing more than 16 minutes per game.

THIS DUNK FROM BRAYDEN BURRIES🤯14 points for the @Bucks rookie off the bench tonight! pic.twitter.com/H3Jk99cKn3

Burries did have one of the highlights of the season so far with a poster dunk over Tristan Enaruna. That game was also the highest-scoring (14 points) game of his so far.

Lendeborg is one of the most entertaining players to watch. You either love him or hate him, but you're still going to watch. It should come as no surprise that it took him exactly one game to talk trash to the opponent, which nearly backfired when Luka Dončić went on to drop 37 points less than 10 days after the season opener.

The highs of Lendeborg's rookie season so far have been fantastic. Even though he had his worst statistical game against the Lakers, he finished with at least 25 points in three consecutive games, including a 31-point, 12-rebound outburst against the Nuggets. Yes, Lendeborg may be the oldest rookie from the first round of the draft, but it's clear to see why the Warriors drafted him. He is already Golden State's second-best player behind Steph Curry, which shouldn't even be that hot of a take. Lendeborg was awesome in a win over the Clippers and scored a career-high 37 points. He should be the co-favorite with Boozer for ROTY.

It's going to be sink-or-swim for Mara, with Chet Holmgren becoming the latest Thunder player to suffer an injury that will sideline him for multiple weeks. Mara logged 28 minutes against the Rockets and finished with seven points, nine rebounds and four blocks. Mara was one of the most efficient scorers at the rim and also one of the top shot blockers in college basketball because of his long 7-foot-3 frame. Mara has a chance to contribute in a larger role with Holmgren out. He's going to be just fine.

Ament was a DNP-CD in Ament's first two games before making his first appearance against the 76ers. Ament has skill and potential but is one of the rawest players drafted in the lottery. The Bucks are bringing him on slowly, which should do wonders for his development. He shot under 40% from the field last season at Tennessee but has been solid in that department (45.8% from the field, 44.4% from 3) in four games. The sample size isn't large enough to give a definitive grade, but Ament has shown signs of improvement since his college days. He has also been solid on the defensive end of the floor.

Steinbach has played in just two games this season, both of which came in garbage time. He played 12 minutes in a 121-81 loss to the Hawks and two minutes against the Wizards last week. Coming into the season, I expected Steinbach to play a larger role. That could still happen later in the season, but the sample size so far isn't large enough to hand out a letter grade.

#2508. Dedan Thomas Jr. leads the way again as No. 10 UH beats Cal in Lake Tahoe Classic

Dedan Thomas Jr. had 20 points and eight assists as No. 10 Houston cruised to a 86-68 victory over Cal on Sunday night at the Caesars Lake Tahoe Classic in Stateline, Nev.

Thomas, a transfer point guard from LSU, was 9-of-15 from the floor to lead the Cougars in scoring for the second straight game.

Joseph Tugler added 16 points and four blocks as the Cougars extended their winning streak against unranked opponents to 42 games.

Guard Chendall Weaver scored six points and had three steals in 15 minutes in his season debut. Weaver, a transfer from Texas seeking a fifth year of eligibility, was granted a temporary restraining order by a Tarrant County district court on Nov. 4.

Weaver sparked UH's early run with an electric 30-second stretch that included a dunk off a missed shot and converted a steal into a fastbreak dunk.

Forward Chase McCarty had three 3-pointers - including two in the game's opening minutes - and 11 points in 12 minutes. McCarty was in the starting lineup after suffering a sprained left knee in the season-opening win against La Salle.

3-Point Goals: 6-16, .375 (McCarty 3-7, D.Thomas 1-1, East 1-1, Gillespie 1-3, Hadnot 0-1, Weaver 0-1, Miller 0-2).

Blocked Shots: 7 (Tugler 4, East 2, Diané).

Turnovers: 9 (Hadnot 2, Tugler 2, D.Thomas, Diané, East, Gillespie, Miller).

Steals: 14 (Miller 3, Weaver 3, D.Thomas 2, Jefferson 2, Tugler 2, Hadnot, McCarty).

3-Point Goals: 9-26, .346 (Cooper 5-8, Yeanay 2-4, Indrusaitis 1-3, Ali 1-5, Ross 0-1, Ruff 0-1, Carr 0-2, Wilkins 0-2).

Turnovers: 16 (Indrusaitis 4, Kocanas 3, Ross 3, Daubaris 2, Wilkins 2, Manyiel Dut, Yeanay).

Steals: 6 (Cooper 2, Ali, Indrusaitis, Manyiel Dut, Ross).

The Cougars (2-0) led by 17 in the first half and pushed their lead to 23 on a few occasions in the second half.

Cal (2-1) trimmed the deficit to 13 on a layup by Jordan Ross with 8:04 remaining.

Delrecco Gillespie added 13 points (6-of-10 shooting) and eight rebounds for the Cougars. UH has won its first two games by an average 28.5 points.

UH finished with seven blocked shots and 14 steals.

Michael Cooper had five 3-pointers and led Cal with 19 points.

#2505. Josh Jacobs fractures finger in Week 9

Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs (finger) suffered a fractured finger in the first quarter of the Week 9 game against the New England Patriots, limiting him to four carries for just five yards.

Head coach Matt LaFleur said after the game that the team is hopeful of finding a way for Jacobs to play through the injury in the future.

Why it Matters: Kaleb Johnson had a big performance with 14 carries, 68 yards and a touchdown with Jacobs departing, and he could be the back to target for fantasy purposes, should Jacobs need to miss time. Pierre Strong also saw eight carries in a complementary role to Johnson.

#2504. Russell Westbrook number retirement: OKC Thunder to hang No. 0 from the rafters in February

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Oklahoma City Thunder will put Russell Westbrook's No. 0 into the rafters at the Paycom Center on Feb. 7, 2027, when they host the New York Knicks, the team announced on Monday.

0 Forever 💙02.07.27 pic.twitter.com/pTqRnespU2

Westbrook retired this offseason after an 18-year career that saw him make nine All-Star teams, nine All-NBA teams and win the 2016-17 MVP award. All but one of those All-Star and All-NBA seasons came as a member of the Thunder; he averaged 23.0 points, 8.4 assists, 7.0 rebounds and 1.8 steals per game across 821 appearances in an Oklahoma City uniform.

"Many players make an impact but only great players leave a legacy. Russell Westbrook's legacy was built both on the court and in the community," general manager Sam Presti said in a statement. "His mindset was relentless, his commitment deep. For all those reasons, Oklahomans consider him one of their own and his number will be raised to the rafters, in Oklahoma City forever."

The Thunder traded Westbrook to the Houston Rockets before the 2019-20 season, but he struggled to stick with a team for long. While he remained productive, he bounced from Houston to Washington to Los Angeles (both the Lakers and Clippers) to Denver to Sacramento before calling it a career, never lasting two full seasons in the same place.

After a rash of injuries in Oklahoma City and with Westbrook's retirement still fresh, some wondered if the Thunder might consider calling in Westbrook for reinforcements on the roster. When asked about that possibility following Jalen Williams' season-ending injury and Cason Wallace's shoulder surgery, Presti insisted he hadn't considered any roster moves at that time.

"I haven't thought about anything relative to the roster spot," Presti said during a press conference last week. "I understand the question, but all I'm really focused on right now is players, getting them the right support, and then helping everybody with our group realize that, you know, we have a tremendous challenge in front of us."

From a basketball perspective, the fit between Westbrook and this current Thunder roster would've perhaps been a bit clunky, but many wondered if OKC still might pursue it as a fitting, emotional send-off for the franchise's favorite son. With the announcement of his jersey retirement, that puts to rest any speculation he'll end his retirement to return to play for the Thunder. Still, he'll get to return to the only team he ever called home long-term -- and the only fan base that ever truly embraced him.

"Let Westbrook be Westbrook" was a favorite saying during his prime years in Oklahoma City, and it's the only place he ever was able to do just that. After Kevin Durant left for the Warriors, Westbrook became the avatar of loyalty in OKC, and the Thunder faithful latched onto their star guard even more after feeling betrayed by Durant.

While it didn't yield the championship Westbrook and Thunder fans hoped for during his tenure, he is the most beloved figure in franchise history for what he did to establish NBA basketball in Oklahoma City and give back to the community. On Feb. 7, he'll get a chance to receive a long-awaited warm welcome back to his adopted home and see the No. 0 get raised to the rafters.

#2503. Pistons vs. Lakers: Austin Reaves pulls a Doncic to beat Detroit

Who needs Luka Doncic when you have the US equivalent from Newark, Arkansas, Austin Reaves? The Los Angeles Lakers guard scored a game-high 43 as his MVP-level teammate rested with a back injury, propelling LA past the Detroit Pistons 121-116.

Honestly, the game had no reason to be as close as it was in the end. The Lakers led 40-14 one basket into the second quarter courtesy of insane shotmaking (hitting 72% from the floor) and an insane amount of Pistons miscues, including having more turnovers (eight) than made baskets (six).

But the Pistons, being the Pistons, weren't about to give up. While Detroit pulled within one point early in the fourth quarter, the Lakers led wire to wire. So while it was only marginally competitive from Detroit's point of view, it was certainly an instructive game. Here are some of the things I learned:

Kevin Huerter is going to be a critical component of the Pistons' rotation this season. In a game where Detroit's entire backcourt didn't really show up to play (both Cade Cunningham and Duncan Robinson were largely no-shows until some fourth-quarter scoring), Huerter was by far the biggest bright spot for the Pistons.

It also happened to be his best game in a Detroit uniform. Huerter hit four three-pointers, scored 24 points overall, and added five rebounds, five assists, five blocks(?!) and two steals. Ever since the Pistons traded for him at the deadline last season, it was clear Huerter makes winning plays, and you were hoping he'd be able to combine that with rediscovering his 3-point shooting stroke from earlier in his career. The early returns indicate the shot might be back, as well as everything that goes with it. After tonight, he's hitting 40% from deep this season.

Detroit's starting front court simply does not work, and it will never work. For as long as Jalen Duren remains sidelined or off the floor this season, this is going to be a significant issue for the Pistons. Duren is ramping back up from a hamstring injury and will be out two more weeks. Detroit has been, and will continue to be able to weather that storm. But it ain't pretty, and any additional time off from Duren will have me significantly worried.

Most will want to pin the blame on the newcomer John Collins, and he has certainly played worse than Reed, but I think it's the combination that brings out the worst in both players. Each is the kind of big man that relies on the gravity from teammates that allows them to use their athleticism to create the chaos that makes them effective. With both of them on the floor, it's two bouncy balls pinging around the floor with no semblance of a plan on how to actually get the ball to the rim. The defense is also bad, and the rebounding is even worse. It's an ugly situation, and it was exacerbated tonight by both men getting out-physicaled by the behemoth seven-footer Walker Kessler. Kessler, the Lakers' big offseason addition, had 12 points and 16 rebounds, including seven on the offensive end. The Lakers also dominated the Pistons in the paint, 58-46.

Again, the lion's share of the blame goes to Collins. He's been quite bad all season, and it's getting less clear by the day how he's going to turn it around and be a positive force for the Pistons. I don't think he's ever met a 50-50 ball he couldn't surrender to the opposition. But the pathway to him playing well lies with sharing the floor with Duren. Get well soon, JD.

The Pistons were correct in trying to give Austin Reaves the bag this offseason. Detroit reportedly was ready to give the wing a max contract this offseason as the second scorer and potential missing piece in a Detroit Pistons title run. Once the Lakers believed the pending RFA had a max offer on the table, they quickly moved to get an agreement to sign him on the eve of free agency so he'd never hit the market.

Reaves was insane tonight. The degree of difficulty on his shots begged belief. He was able to create space, get balanced, and score at all three levels. It was a sight to behold, and he was by far the best player on the floor for either team tonight.

Daniss has that dog in him, especially under two scenarios: 1. There is an impending buzzer. 2. He feels like his team is getting punked. Jenkins was truly the other hero of the game behind Huerter. He hit yet another buzzer-beater tonight, and he scored a career-high 31 points. When the Pistons were down huge, Jenkins got that look in his eye, as if to say, "This is not going to happen."

From there, Jenkins started firing away from deep, and he was hitting. In the end, he canned eight three-pointers. He was also the ONLY Pistons player to go to the free-throw line more than once in the game. Really, Jenkins is like a better version of Marcus Sasser. He's got scoring in his blood, and he's more of an off-guard than a point guard, despite being stuck in a point guard's body. He's got three inches on Sasser and better floor vision, so he's better overall and can cosplay as a point guard better than Sass, but Jenkins works best in this Pistons lineup when he's not running the offense.

The referees love the Lakers. Nothing else needs to be said.

#2501. Why Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg was benched after being 'peer pressured' into chasing 40 against Clippers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Golden State Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has been a revelation to open his NBA career. Through his first seven games, he's putting up historic numbers, and he somehow keeps one-upping himself. On Sunday, he played his best game yet: 37 points on 85% true shooting. He made six of his 11 3-pointers and added six assists. He was outrageously good, as he has been all season, save for the Lakers game last Friday in which he was properly hazed by Luka Dončić.

Other than that, it's been nothing but buckets for Lendeborg, who, given how easily all this has seemingly come for him, perhaps got a little ahead of himself by chasing the 40-point round number on Sunday with a couple of, shall we say, questionable shots at the end.

Steve Kerr saw it, and with 2:14 to play, he benched his rookie as the Clippers were starting to make a desperate run, cutting a 21-point Warriors lead to eight over a two-minute span during which Lendeborg missed three 3-pointers, two of which were total chuck jobs.

"He would've had 40 if we had just kept playing [normally]," Kerr said after the game. "The NBA game these days can change like that. We all know that. Almost every night, there's a 25-point lead that is overcome.

"The game changed when all the guys on the bench were yelling at Yax to get 40. He launched three kind of bad shots. A lesson is, if you just keep playing, then you stay in rhythm, you stay in flow, the ball moves, and then the game becomes much easier. I think that's the lesson for him and for our team.

"But everybody loves Yax. Everybody wanted him to get 40. They were urging him to shoot from the bench, and It got us out of rhythm a little bit."

As soon as Lendeborg went to the bench and the Warriors got back to business, De'Antony Melton, who was a stud all night, buried back-to-back 3s to put the game back on ice. It was a great night for the Warriors, who've won four straight after opening 0-3, and for Lendeborg, who continues to be a total open book who is more than willing to admit to his mistakes and vow not to repeat them, as he did after the Lakers debacle when he took full accountability for "wetting the bed."

Yaxel Lendeborg was chasing 40 points late and it let the Clippers back into it briefly. He said he fell into peer pressure. It was his lesson of the night: "I've never been a stat chaser...I'm a guy that loves ethical hoops."Full Yaxel + Steve Kerr soundbite pic.twitter.com/5Lyo3CVXMb

"I've never been a stat chaser in my life," Yaxel said after he was benched on Sunday. "So, I mean, just falling into peer pressure like I did just now was pretty much bad on my part. Especially just, I'm a guy that loves, like, ethical hoops. I'm a guy that loves efficient basketball, and I didn't do that for the last two to three minutes. So, it's kind of, like, bad on my part. Next time I definitely won't do that again. If it comes to me, it does. If I don't get it, then I wasn't meant to get it that day. So, I'm gonna be way better next time."

Lendeborg elaborated on the peer pressure aspect of the chase, which, frankly, anyone can understand. You're a rookie and you're going off and your teammates are all cheering you on to keep shooting. The game, you think, is in the bag. Any player in that situation would've let a few more shots go.

"De'Anthony Melton went up to me and said, 'Hey, man you need to get 40. You're three points away,'" Lendeborg said. "And I'm like, 'Nah, It's all good.' He just peer pressured me into doing it. ... He said he's gonna give me the ball, and he literally was holding it just to give me the ball. I'm like, all right, fine, I'll shoot it,' and I missed. I tried to tell him 'no, no, no,' and now Will [Richards] came over [to me saying], 'you gotta do it, you gotta do it.'

"So everybody was just egging me on and I kind of just fell into it. But I know next time I'm just going to play in the flow of the game, because [the Clippers] came down and made like four threes in a row and we almost lost the game because of that. So next time I'm never doing that again."

#2500. Buccaneers tie it late, but Caleb Williams hits big play to set up game-winning field goal for Bears

Chicago Bears wide receiver Luther Burden III (10) runs to score a touchdown against Tampa Bay Buccaneers cornerback Zyon McCollum (27). (AP Photo/David Banks)

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers had chances to beat one of the NFL's hottest teams on Sunday night. They just didn't do enough to actually win the game.

Between Buccaneers coach Todd Bowles settling for three short field goals and multiple offensive mistakes including a pick 6 from Baker Mayfield, the Buccaneers let the Chicago Bears escape on a night in which Caleb Williams threw four interceptions. Tampa Bay tied it late but Williams answered with one big pass to tight end Colston Loveland, which set up a game-winning field goal as time expired. Chicago won 27-24 and the Buccaneers will have plenty of regrets over letting one slip away.

The Bears improved to 7-2 but their offense got shut down and made mistakes to help Tampa Bay stay in the game. But it wasn't enough, after falling behind 14-0 early, to be passive.

Tampa Bay showed that to win a big game on the road, you have to get more aggressive to pull the upset. The Buccaneers played well, stayed in the game, and ultimately went home with a loss.

The Bears got off to a hot start and it looked like they might blow out the Buccaneers. They gave up a 9-yard touchdown catch to Rome Odunze and a 56-yard touchdown catch to Luther Burden III. Two Chicago possessions into the game, Tampa Bay trailed 14-0.

Then the turnovers started. The Bears had the ball inside Tampa Bay's 10-yard line on their third drive but rookie receiver Zavion Thomas took an unnecessary roughness penalty that pushed Chicago back. The next play Caleb Williams threw an interception. That seemed to get in Williams' head. The play after the Buccaneers got stuffed on a quarterback sneak on a fourth-and-1 in their own territory, Williams threw a touchdown off his back foot for his second interception in two passes. He had thrown one interception all season before Sunday, in 158 attempts. After Chicago got a field goal, Williams threw another one up for grabs and Tampa Bay had its third interception of the night.

Tampa Bay didn't fully take advantage, though they stayed in the game. Twice, Buccaneers coach Todd Bowles decided to settle for field goals close to the goal line instead of being aggressive with his team trailing. The first time the Buccaneers kicked a 25-yard field goal on fourth-and-4 at the Bears' 7-yard line. Late in the first half the Bucs got the ball to the 3-yard line and had time for one more play before halftime, but they took a short field goal again.

The Buccaneers were still in the game when they scored early in the third quarter, but still trailed 17-13 and they had let many opportunities pass them by. But Chicago couldn't put them away.

Williams threw another interception on a deflected pass in the third quarter. He had never thrown three interceptions in an NFL game and suddenly he had four on Sunday night. But again, Tampa Bay struggled to take advantage of it.

Baker Mayfield never seemed to notice cornerback Jaylon Johnson lurking underneath in coverage and threw an interception to him, which Johnson returned for a 67-yard touchdown and a 24-13 Chicago lead.

But Tampa Bay's defense was remarkable in the second half. The Buccaneers allowed just one first down in the first 28 minutes after halftime. That kept the game close.

In the fourth quarter, Bowles passed on going for it on fourth-and-4 at Chicago's 12-yard line to settle for a short field goal for the third time in the game. That cut the Bears' lead to 24-16 but it still required the Buccaneers stopping Chicago, putting together a touchdown drive, making the two-point conversion, keeping the Bears from winning it regulation and then Tampa Bay winning the game in overtime. They started checking those boxes though.

Burden lost a fumble on a third down reception that would have been short of the first down, and Tampa Bay recovered on the Bears' 17-yard line with 3:38 left. Two runs by Bucky Irving got the Bucs into the end zone and Mayfield scrambled up the middle for the two-point conversion and a tie game.

But the Buccaneers had only tied it and Chicago had ample time to answer. Williams got the drive going and then the Buccaneers lost Loveland in coverage. He gained 38 yards. After a half in which the Bears barely moved the ball, one big play was enough to give them a shot at the field goal and the win.

Cairo Santos hit the game-winner and Chicago got the win, knowing that the Buccaneers handed them plenty of chances to take it at the end.

Cairo Santos drills it from 38 yards out, and the Bears have survived a wild "Sunday Night Football" outing at Soldier Field.

Caleb Williams is back. He just connected with Coleston Loveland for a 38-yard gain, and the Bears are suddenly in field goal range.

Bucky Irving has found the end zone for the second time tonight! The 2-point attempt was good, too. Baker Mayfield just kept it himself.

We're all tied up, 24-24, with 2:51 left.

Luther Burden was down for quite some time after that fumble, and needed help getting off the field. He eventually walked off on his own.

They threw a screen pass on third down to try and seal the win, but Luther Burden lost the ball.

The Bucs now have it back inside the red zone and can tie it up.

The Bucs couldn't convert on third-and-long, so they opted to punt it away. They do still have two timeouts, so a quick stop here would give them a shot.

This was the first of back-to-back sacks for the Bears defense, and the Bucs are looking at third and long again.

Austin Booker got Baker Mayfield by the facemask while sacking him on third down. That's a huge penalty that keeps Tampa's drive alive.

Add another punt to this list, and it's remarkable the Bears are leading.

The Buccaneers will take over at their own 15 with 8:03 left in the game. They're running out of time to tie this thing up.

Baker Mayfield got the Bucs into scoring position, but their drive stalled out. A 35-yard field goal works, too, and we've got an 8-point game.

Neither team on the last five drives has had a single first down. The Bears are punting it away again near the end of the third.

They tried to fake the punt, too, but got called for a false start.

Kalif Raymond just muffed a punt return after a quick stop again, but he managed to recover the ball to stop the turnover.

Baker Mayfield just threw a pick-6 on his very first play after Caleb Williams' interception, and he took a pretty big hit at the goal line.

Jaylon Johnson gets the touchdown, and Chicago is up 24-13 now late in the third. Wow.

Make that four interceptions for Caleb Williams now, though that one wasn't entirely his fault. He tried to find Luther Burden, but the ball was deflected up and right into Alex Anzalone's arms.

Well, maybe not. A holding penalty doomed that drive for the Bucs, and Baker Mayfield is limping off after missing Egbuka deep on third down.

That's the stop Chicago needed. Now we'll see if the Bears offense can get anything going.

That punt ended up going about 25 yards after it was just barely blocked at the line, so Tampa will start in Bears territory.

Florida State's starting 11 included Ryder Ajeto, Wrianna Hudson, Shaneil Buckley, Joelle Jung, Peyton McGovern, Nawreen Ahmad, Tanner Strickland, Bridget Mutipula, Janet Okeke, Grace Hoytink and Kate Ockene.

Virginia broke through at 38:09 when Allie Ross scored off an assist from Ella Carter, giving the Cavaliers a 1-0 lead.

#2497. Five things we learned from Victor Wembanyama's '60 Minutes' interview, including why he loves going barefoot

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It is increasingly rare in the NBA (and professional sports as a whole) for a star athlete to sit down for an extended, on-the-record interview. While athletes have found other means of communicating with fans, such interviews can offer rare, less-filtered glimpses into what the player is going through both on and off the court.

Few players in any sport can say they've had a more eventful last few years than Victor Wembanyama. The San Antonio Spurs star reached his first NBA Finals last season and, in the process became a villain to fans across the world rooting for the New York Knicks to end their 53-year championship drought. He ultimately fell short in that matchup, but is now ascending to his seemingly inevitable place as the future face of the NBA. With the 2026-27 season only just beginning, Wembanyama sat down with CBS News' "60 Minutes" to discuss his career thus far. Here are five highlights:

Sponsorships are a standard component of the superstar experience. Wembanyama has been intentionally choosy about who and what he has aligned himself with. In the past, he has made it clear that he would never work with a soda company, for instance, because he does not want to promote unhealthy products. In Sunday's interview, he took aim at athletes promoting different vices.

"I think as an NBA player, and if you're amongst the stars of this league, you really make your career whatever you want to make it," he said. "Of course, you're always going to do your best on the court, the best that you can. But on the side, you can choose to be the influencer, you can choose to be the philanthropist, you can choose to be the guy who's gonna promote gambling and alcohol. You can choose whatever you want."

When asked what choice he has made, Wembanyama reiterated that health is his guiding principle. "I think my choice isn't final because I'm still growing as a person," he said. "But I want to promote healthy things, and by healthy, I don't just mean the food, but healthy habits, things that make people's lives better. And in the future, things that also make society better."

The public perception of Wembanyama changed quite a bit over the course of a single postseason. He was one of the league's breakout stars last season, and his consistent success over the widely disliked Oklahoma City Thunder earned him quite a bit of admiration from casual fans. However, his hard fouls, first in the second round against the Minnesota Timberwolves, and then later, of course, against the Knicks, turned him into a villain overnight. While Wembanyama claimed he wasn't paying attention to that noise during the Finals, he did learn from it after the fact.

"It showed my limits more than anything else," Wembanyama said. "Going out there, you need to play basketball, you don't need to beat the shit out of people. If you want to win at least." Had the Finals lasted beyond five games, he might have learned the lesson in more convincing fashion.

In Game 5, Wembanyama committed a foul on Jalen Brunson that many argued was flagrant after the fact, but because the Knicks ended the series then and there, the NBA was not forced to review it. Wembanyama was just one flagrant foul point away from a suspension for a hypothetical Game 6 at Madison Square Garden. Now, Wembanyama wants to make sure he doesn't put himself in that situation again.

Shoes are perhaps the single most important piece of equipment in a basketball player's arsenal, yet whenever possible, Wembanyama prefers not to wear them. "I try to walk barefoot as much as I can, and wear minimalistic shoes," he explained. For him, it's a matter of health.

"Because big men have always had feet problems," Wembanyama said, alluding to the NBA's lengthy history of injury-prone centers. "I also find more and more that feet are responsible for so much more that goes on. It's funny because I was just talking to a rookie. I went to practice barefoot and he sees me walk in without shoes and he goes, 'I did not know you could just not wear shoes.'"

Wembanyama believes that "if you've got good foot strength, which brings a good foot posture, everything else can level up the right way. Knee, hip, back and everything." Thus far, his methods seem to be working. His longest absence in the NBA came as the result of a blood clot in his shoulder, and while he has dealt with some of the same lower body injuries that many players are enduring in the pace-and-space era, he managed to maintain awards eligibility in both his first and third seasons. He has not yet missed a game this year.

Wembanyama has lived in the United States for more than three years now, yet he acknowledges how atypical his American existence has been. "When they ask me what it's like to live in the U.S., my answer is always, well, I don't know. I don't live a normal life in the U.S.," he said. "I live the life of an athlete, a rich person, the life of somebody that's gonna have everything taken care of no matter what I do, really. It's not the life of a regular American. It's the best country to be an athlete in."

That atypical experience has given him a unique perspective on life in the United States, and he sees both pros and cons compared to what he grew up with in France. "Good is how it feels like you're never judged for being ambitious," he argued. "Bad, I would say, I think the social interactions are more shallow here. Not as in-depth as they are in other countries."

Wembanyama is hardly the first foreign-born star to thrive in the NBA, but he's on pace to outshine all those who came before him. The NBA has obviously had plenty of international MVPs and champions, but it has never had a foreign face. Eventually, Wembanyama is expected to stand alone atop the sport, once the old guard of legends like LeBron James and Stephen Curry retire. That puts him in a somewhat unique position to attempt to influence the way stars conduct themselves moving forward. He is already seemingly attempting to do that in the way he chooses sponsors, and only time will tell how much more of his perspective will trickle down to his NBA contemporaries.

Wembanyama has never been shy about how excited he was to land with the Spurs. He called it "a winner's franchise," and cited both the team's history with French players and the presence of "the greatest coach of all time" as draws even before San Antonio won the 2023 NBA Draft Lottery. While that coach, Gregg Popovich, has since retired after suffering a stroke, Wembanyama got to start his career with Popovich on the sideline, and he explained that his greatest lesson was "about humility."

"He often said something when we were in film: after a win, you're rarely as good as you thought you were. And after a loss, you're rarely as bad as you thought you were," Wembanyama said.

That is a lesson that will have to persist this season, as the Spurs attempt to pick up the pieces following their Finals loss to New York. San Antonio blew double-digit leads in all four of its losses in that series, and the film will inevitably showcase many of the ways in which they were deficient against the Knicks. But the Spurs got to the Finals in the first place, well ahead of schedule, and while they should internalize what didn't work, they should hold onto what did.

It certainly seems as though they've done that this season, winning four straight after losing their first two games of the season. The Spurs are currently the championship favorite following a rash of injuries to the Thunder, and maintaining an even keel across the season will be essential in ensuring that they maintain that favored status.

#2494. Three notable decisions from NBA's rookie-scale extension deadline: Thunder seemingly give up on lottery pick

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Normally, the NBA's deadline for teams to pick up team options on their rookie-scale contracts is Halloween. As the end of October came on a weekend this year, however, it was pushed to Monday. This deadline is usually relatively uneventful. Former first-round picks living up to expectations, or with obvious paths to improvement in the near future, have their third- and fourth-year options picked up. Obvious busts tend not to.

Of course, teams inevitably get these decisions wrong from time to time, and that sends promising players to unrestricted free agency at the end of the season in question. The most notable recent example came in 2021, when the Phoenix Suns declined their third-year option on Jalen Smith, whom they'd selected at No. 10 overall ahead of players like Devin Vassell and Tyrese Haliburton less than a year earlier. Smith has since grown into one of the NBA's better shooting big men for the Chicago Bulls.

I bring this up because a handful of notable team options were declined ahead of Monday's deadline, setting some interesting prospects up for unrestricted free agency next summer. The NBA is more financially cautious than it has ever been thanks to the aprons, forcing teams to make hard decisions on young players before their futures are fully written. There will inevitably be more Jalen Smiths in the years to come, and a few declined options from the past few days stand out as candidates.

There's a degree of validation that comes with being drafted by the Oklahoma City Thunder. Sam Presti thought Nikola Topić was worth the No. 12 overall pick in 2024, and while Presti is hardly infallible, he's the NBA's best general manager by a wide margin and his instincts are usually worth imitation. Oklahoma City didn't decline Topić's 2027-28 option because he's played poorly. They declined it because he's barely played at all.

He missed his rookie season with a torn ACL. He missed most of his second getting treated for testicular cancer, only appearing briefly in 10 games. He has not yet played this season because of back surgery. It is entirely possible that Topić simply never stays healthy enough to reach his potential as a player. It is also entirely possible, especially on a Thunder team that suddenly needs minutes wherever they can find them, that he starts living up to that potential the moment he returns to floor.

Oklahoma City's injuries represent the greatest opportunity of Topić's career. The team that drafted him averaged 66 wins in his first two seasons. There weren't going to be many minutes available for him anyway. Now, if he can just make it back onto the court, he should get real on-ball reps for the team with the best player-development track record in basketball. He can set himself up for a real opportunity in unrestricted free agency next summer.

The Thunder were never going to be able to afford him long-term considering all of their other obligations, so in that sense, they've arguably done Topić a favor. If they'd picked up his option and then cap dumped him later, he might have wound up in a bad basketball situation. Now, he has the rest of the season to show what he can do and the freedom to shop his services to the teams that need them most.

Guard minutes were readily available for the Utah Jazz over the last two seasons. Isaiah Collier took plenty of them, averaging over 25 minutes per game in each of his first two seasons. Even with Darryn Peterson in the fold this year and Ace Bailey taking on a bigger role next to Keyonte George, Collier has still been featured pretty heavily by backup standards. Case in point: through six games, he is averaging the most minutes on the roster (18.5) of anyone who has not yet started a game.

Yet the Jazz surprisingly decided to decline his option for the 2027-28 campaign on Monday. What this means for the Jazz next season still isn't clear. Utah still has plenty of room below next season's projected luxury tax, but that space could evaporate quickly if they elect to re-sign restricted free agent Brice Sensabaugh and/or use a mid-level exception. Perhaps the Jazz want to seek out a veteran backup. They may also prefer to minimize their investment in ball-handlers to ensure that both George and Peterson play on the ball when the other rests. The Jazz have plenty of shot-creation in the front court. They can afford to be stingy at backup point guard.

Collier arrived in the NBA as a high-level playmaker. His scoring and defense just haven't kept up. But he was once the No. 1 recruit in his high school class, and there's plenty of tape on him already for other teams to study. The talent is here even if the role potentially wouldn't have been in Utah.

Tidjane Salaün was the highest draft 2024 Draft pick (No. 6 overall) to have his fourth-year option declined, but that probably works in favor of a potential reunion between him and the Charlotte Hornets over the summer if both sides want to pursue one. When a player has a rookie-scale option declined, his original team can still re-sign him in free agency ... but only up to the salary he would have made on that option. Salaün's fourth-year salary would have been $10.4 million or so.

That's a much heftier figure than later picks, and it creates a bit of a win-win scenario for the Hornets. If Salaün doesn't live up to that figure, they aren't forced to pay it to him and could try to keep him at a lower rate. If he does, however, then they are at least getting a productive player at a scarce position for this season. If nothing else, that's a valuable trade chip at the deadline.

Salaün's overall minutes have gone down in each of his NBA seasons thus far, but he's playing better than he ever has in that smaller role this year. That's not saying all that much, but his combination of physical traits, theoretical ball-handling and shooting and willingness to play hard at least offer the outline of a useful, all-around wing. This is a player archetype that teams are usually eager to take chances on. Whether it's with Charlotte or somebody else, Salaün will probably get another chance.

#2492. 4 Huge Takeaways After Reaves Leads Shorthanded Lakers Past Pistons

The Los Angeles Lakers entered Sunday night's matchup as one of the top teams in the West with arguably the most in-form player in the league leading them. With Luka Doncic sidelined, concerns about L.A.'s chances of beating the Detroit Pistons seemed justified. Surprisingly, the Lakers dispelled all of these doubts.

With a 121-116 win, the Los Angeles Lakers improved to 9-2 on the season, placing first in the West while notching their fifth consecutive win. While Doncic's absence was undoubtedly a factor, Lakers' star Austin Reaves showed exactly what he is capable of.

From establishing a 26-point lead early in the game to defending against the Pistons' furious comeback charge, the Purple and Gold displayed remarkable tenacity and fortitude. Additionally, with a dominant 43-point outing to lead L.A. past Detroit, Reaves showed how deep the Lakers truly are this season.

Reaves' performance was undoubtedly the most noteworthy aspect of Sunday night's outing. However, with several key developments accompanying this, examine four key takeaways from L.A.'s win over Detroit.

The last few seasons have really seen Austin Reaves transform into a star-caliber player. With some spectacular offensive displays early last season as well, Reaves has demonstrated his ability to be a reliable scoring option. Despite this, there appear to be many who doubt it.

After facing some early-season struggles, especially in light of his sizable contract extension, these comments would seem justified. Still, the 28-year-old proved naysayers wrong with his season-high scoring night against the Pistons.

Needless to say, this is an extremely positive sign for the Lakers, who can be over-reliant on Doncic for creation. While Reaves lacks his running mate's passing and playmaking ability, Sunday night's display showed that he can certainly compensate for it with his scoring.

With 43 points, five rebounds, and four assists on 14-27 FG and 4-6 3PT FG, Reaves had it going from everywhere. With some timely three-pointers in the fourth quarter, even while facing some tough defense, the guard showed exactly why he earned the Purple and Gold's trust.

Walker Kessler has arguably been one of the most consistent performers for the Lakers this season outside of Luka Doncic. Having established himself as an elite big man, Kessler continues to dominate as a defensive anchor and a rebounder. Unfortunately, there are some issues that may demand some attention.

On Sunday night, Kessler notched another double-double of 12 points, 16 rebounds, one steal, and three blocks, showcasing his overall involvement in the win. While his 16 rebounds and three blocks are eye-catching, his scoring on 5-10 shooting isn't necessarily a positive sign.

In his debut performance for the Lakers, Walker Kessler notched a monster 26 points on 12-12 shooting from the field. Barring a few outliers, he has maintained this degree of efficiency, but it is worth noting that his shot attempts are wildly inconsistent.

In games played with Luka Doncic, Kessler often finds himself getting more touches on the ball, which results in marginally more shot attempts. In Doncic's absence, however, he seems more tentative, which is only exacerbated by the fact that he isn't utilized as much.

Kessler's impact as a lob threat was not as prominent against the Pistons on Sunday. While this could be attributed to Reaves' decision-making ability as a point guard, one could argue that getting the big man more involved offensively could help L.A. expand its scoring options.

A surprising development over the past few games has been Jarred Vanderbilt's increased involvement and playing time in the rotation. Before the start of the season, Vanderbilt was perceived as a clear trade option who may not have a place in the Lakers' current lineup. Now, however, he may have genuine upside.

As a scorer, Jarred Vanderbilt remains limited. With virtually no "bag" and a questionable shot from deep, he struggles to contribute consistently. However, it is becoming clear that his presence on the floor addresses the Lakers' need for rebounding.

On Sunday night, Vanderbilt was one of the most active players on the glass, securing 10 rebounds, two of which were offensive. Pairing this with his defensive effort and playmaking, and suddenly, the Lakers have another solid rotation piece.

At this juncture, Jarred Vanderbilt seems like a more impactful player than Sandro Mamukelashvili, who appears to be in a bit of a slump. Given Vanderbilt's defensive and rebounding upside, the Lakers could consider giving him more playing time depending on the matchups.

Aside from all the positive takeaways from Sunday night's game, the winning effort also highlighted an underlying issue with Quentin Grimes.

When the Purple and Gold signed him this summer, Quentin Grimes seemed like a promising addition with notable two-way upside. Having showcased his talents as a scorer during his stint with the Philadelphia 76ers, the fans had good reason to be excited. Unfortunately, it is safe to say that he hasn't lived up to expectations.

With Doncic sidelined, Grimes was promoted to the starting lineup with the intention of being a reliable second option next to Austin Reaves. While his early outburst of 10 points in the first quarter suggested that he was on track to fulfill this role, his offensive production came to a grinding halt by the second.

Before the game against Detroit, Grimes was averaging 7.6 points, 2.7 rebounds, and 2.7 assists per game while shooting 45.3% from the field and 21.4% shooting from deep. In many ways, this makes his 12-point outing look solid. Still, given his potential, along with his status as a key rotation piece, L.A. will need him to find his groove again.

#2491. MLB rumors: Mets' Bo Bichette makes contract decision, familiar All-Star back on trade block

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only two days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

As expected, Mets infielder Bo Bichette has picked up his $42 million player option for 2027, reports The Athletic. He holds another $42 million player option for 2028. Still only 28, Bichette had a poor first season in Queens, posting a .702 OPS with 18 home runs while showing growing pains as he transitioned from shortstop over to third base.

For now, the Mets are set on the infield with Bichette at third, Francisco Lindor at short, and Marcus Semien at second. They must figure out first base, and it is possible they will make a trade to shake up that veteran infield. Moving Semien would be ideal, but it may not be doable. Lindor's name figures to pop up in trade rumors against this offseason.

The Diamondbacks are expected to listen to offers for second baseman Ketel Marte, reports the Arizona Republic. The D-backs entertained trade offers last offseason, but were unable to find a match. Marte has full no-trade protection and can direct where he lands, if he wants to leave Arizona at all. His desire to change teams is unknown.

Marte, 33, had a down year by his standards in 2026. He also went AWOL in August, prompting the D-backs to put him on the restricted list. Manager Torey Lovullo later revealed it was the fourth straight season Marte missed a game without permission. Beyond the on-field fit, teams will have to weigh the potential clubhouse impact and headaches.

The Seibu Lions in Japan will make right-hander Kaima Taira available to MLB teams via the posting system this offseason, the team announced Friday. The posting is expected to be made official in the coming days. Once that happens, Taira will have 45 days to negotiate and sign with an MLB team, otherwise he will return to Japan in 2027.

We ranked Taira as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason. Here's our write-up:

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man.

Taira, 27 next month, threw 146 innings with a 1.36 ERA and 141 strikeouts this past season. He actually had higher ERAs as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, though he has been excellent throughout his career in Japan, and has the bat-missing power stuff that tends to translate well to MLB. Taira figures to be highly sought after in the coming weeks.

The trading season resumed Thursday and the Red Sox were involved in the offseason's first two trades. First, they sent utility man Nate Eaton to the Athletics for minor-league righty Jareth Rayo, the team announced. The A's recently named former Red Sox assistant general manager Taylor Smith their new president of baseball operations. His first move was bringing in Eaton, a player he's presumably familiar with given their overlapping time in Boston.

Next, the Red Sox traded infielder Tsung-Che Cheng to the Tigers for cash, the team announced. Cheng, 25, is a glove-first utility man who appeared in 14 games with Boston this past season. Both the Cheng and Eaton trades open up 40-man roster spots for the Red Sox, who still must open three more spots to accommodate their seven players on the 60-day injured list. They must be activated no later than this coming Monday.

Draymond Green made it to November (barely) before earning his first ejection of the 2026-27 NBA season.

On Monday night, Green took exception to getting knocked over by Phoenix Suns center Khaman Maluach posting up in transition and got up and tackled Maluach, wrapping him up with both arms and throwing him to the ground -- Maluach still made a basket for an and-1. Bassey's 19 points in 22 minutes off the bench on Monday night equals Green's 19 points in 159 minutes of play this season. Green does lead the Warriors in assists (6.3 per game), and the offense hums around him with Curry and rookie star Yaxel Lendeborg combining for more than 50 points per game.

With the win, Golden State improved to 5-3 on the season and now sits in seventh in the Western Conference standings early in the season as the Warriors try to claw their way back to the playoffs for the first time in three seasons.

#2489. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

Sunday night's first drive was Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams versus Todd Bowles and his defense. Ben Johnson versus most would be a mismatch and in the game's opening drive that looked to be the case as Tampa Bay fans had to watch Chicago coast down the field and into Tampa Bay's end zone for ten first score of the game. Early concerns for Todd Bowles may stem, not only from the results of the drive (seven points allowed), but also from the fact that Caleb Williams consistently broke outside of the pocket without any noticeable restriction. 7-0, Bears.

The Buccaneers' first six snaps all went to Bucky Irving before Zac Robinson remembered other players play for the Tampa Bay Buccaneers— The other player targeted? Cade Otton. Third and long and Baker Mayfield scrambled his way around the pocket buying time before eventually directing Kenny Gainwell downfield for a 44 yard gain.

Converting turnovers into points are a necessity, however, Tampa converted the turnover into an awkward QB sneak for a failed fourth down conversion.

Taking possession back in field goal range, Williams did it again— Rather Tampa's defense did it again. Zyon McCollum followed Tykee Smith's interception with one of his own. The Bucs' offense was still struggling to offense so naturally a punt would follow. After the Bucs wasted each of their defense's forced turnovers, Chicago knocked through a field goal— 17-3, Bears.

Baker Mayfield and the Bucs' offense got themselves back across a first down marker for the first time in quite while as Emeka Egbuka scooped a low pass over the middle, ticking the first half down to the two-minute warning. #2487. Astros hire Randy Flores as new general manager as offseason filled with questions begins in Houston

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros' search for a new head of baseball operations has ended with the hiring of Randy Flores as general manager. The 51-year-old Flores had been an assistant general manager with the St. Louis Cardinals. In Houston, Flores replaces Dana Brown, who was let go in late August. Flores becomes the fourth head of baseball operations to serve under Astros owner Jim Crane.

"Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," Crane said in a statement released by the club. "Throughout the entire interview process, we've been thoroughly impressed with Randy and his background in scouting and player acquisition. We're happy to welcome Randy and his family to the Astros and we can't wait to get to work on bringing another championship to Houston."

Added Flores: "I am excited and grateful for this amazing opportunity. The Astros have a long winning tradition under Jim Crane, and I look forward to contributing to the success.  I want to thank the Cardinals organization for the opportunities and support that made this next chapter possible. My family and I are excited to make Houston home."

Flores for roughly a decade served as scouting director for the Cardinals and was tasked with running their draft. He added the assistant GM title in 2018 and saw his portfolio of responsibilities expand within the last year.

Flores takes over an Astros organization beset by uncertainty. With an aging roster and after several key departures over the years, the Astros have seen their season-long win total decline for four straight years. This past season, the Astros eked out the American League Central title but finished with a .500 record and a negative run differential. In terms of success and roster strength, they're a long way from their dynasty years of 2017-22. It's not certain whether the Astros moving forward will try to squeeze out another season of relevance or embrace a rebuild, but either path will have its challenges.

Speaking of challenges, Crane and his trusted advisor Jeff Bagwell have been an increasingly meddlesome presence in recent years, and it's unclear to what degree Flores will have autonomy in his role. Whatever the future holds, Flores' first major decision is filling the managerial vacancy. After the end of the regular season, Crane opted not to renew the contract of former manager Joe Espada.

Prior to beginning his front office career, Flores spent parts of eight seasons in the majors as a left-handed reliever. In 2006, he earned a World Series ring as a member of that Cardinals team.

#2483. MLB rumors: Padres decline option on key rotation piece, Korean star to be posted

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only four days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Sunday's hot stove happenings.

San Diego's top two starters are now free agents. Two days after Michael King exercised an opt-out clause to become a free agent, the Padres declined their $14 million club option on Nick Pivetta, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Had the Padres picked up the option, Pivetta would have held an $18 million player option for 2028. That surely factored into the team's decision.

Pivetta, 34 in February, missed roughly five months with a flexor strain this past season. He returned late in the season and pitched reasonably well in six starts spanning September and the postseason. The San Diego Union-Tribune notes the Padres still have concerns about Pivetta's elbow, but could re-sign him to a new contract with a lower salary and/or no player option.

San Diego signed Pivetta to what amounted to a two-year, $23 million contact with two players options in February 2025. The flexor strain triggered an injury clause that converted the 2027 player option into a club option. We ranked Pivetta as the offseason's 43rd-best free agent.

As expected, the Orioles have declined their $20 million club option for center fielder Luis Robert Jr., reports ESPN. They will pay him a $2 million buyout, so it was functionally an $18 million decision. Robert suffered a hamstring injury and played only three games with the O's after being claimed off waivers from the Mets in late September.

Now 29, Robert again had multiple stints on the injured list this past season. He continued to punish lefties and play solid center field defense when healthy, but injuries have limited him to only 271 of 489 possible regular-season games from 2024-26. We did not rank Robert among our top 50 free agents, though he is an interesting upside play given his age.

The Hanwha Eagles of the Korea Baseball Organization will post star third baseman Si-Hwan Roh for MLB teams this offseason, reports Yonhap News Agency. Roh signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and $23 million), though as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the team once his MLB stint is over.

Roh, 26, has been one of the KBO's best players the last several years. He hit .283/.360/.505 with 29 home runs in 2026, and has averaged 35 home runs per 162 games since 2023. Roh is considered a reliable but unspectacular defender at third, plus he has first base experience as well. This free agent class is very thin at the hot corner. Roh should generate a good deal of interest.

KBO players get a 30-day negotiating window once officially posted. If Roh does not sign with an MLB team during the 30-day window, he will return to the Eagles. It's possible that Roh, a right-handed hitter, will eclipse his $23 million guarantee with the Eagles over just a handful of years with an MLB team.

The Astros have acquired Triple-A righty reliever Evan Reifert from the Rays for cash, reports the Tampa Bay Times. Houston is likely to add him to their 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. The Rays did not have the roster space to do that, so they traded for cash rather than lose him for nothing. Reifert, 27, has an excellent slider and used it to strike out 81 batters in 58 Triple-A innings in 2026. He should spend time in Houston's bullpen next season.
