#2482. Mahomes overcomes injury scare in Chiefs win as Burrow shines in Madrid

Three-time Super Bowl champion Patrick Mahomes overcame an injury scare to lift Kansas City over the New York Jets on Sunday while Joe Burrow sparked Cincinnati to victory over Atlanta in Madrid.

Two-time NFL Most Valuable Player Mahomes completed 23-of-31 passes for 242 yards and two touchdowns in the Chiefs' 35-12 triumph over the Jets.

Burrow completed 24-of-29 passes for 271 yards and three touchdowns and ran for another score in Cincinnati's 34-17 victory, the Bengals' fourth triumph in a row.

At Kansas City, Mahomes suffered a right elbow injury and lost a fumble in the second quarter after being sacked by Jets rookie defender David Bailey, but his 120 passing yards and two touchdown throws gave the Chiefs a 14-12 halftime lead.

Mahomes directed touchdown drives of 60 and 82 yards in the third quarter and 57 yards in the fourth and said the elbow was not a factor "once I got it warmed up a little bit."

"It's doing good," Mahomes said of his right elbow. "It's part of playing football. You get hit, you've got to bounce back and we were able to get it loosened back up and we went back out there and played.

"A couple of errant throws early in the second half. My guys rallied behind me. They ran the ball well in the second half. My offensive line did a great job protecting me and then I threw when I needed to."

Kenneth Walker ran 18 times for 102 yards and a touchdown and caught four passes for 41 yards and two touchdowns for the Chiefs (6-2).

The Bengals improved to 6-2, level with idle Pittsburgh atop the AFC North division ahead of their showdown next week.

"The sky is the limit when we play like this. This is how we need to attack every game going forward," said wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase, who made 10 catches for 155 yards and a touchdown.

"Intense impact," Burrow said of Chase. "He was unbelievable."

"He does a good job getting out of the pocket and making scramble plays, keeping the play alive," Chase said. "That's why he's one of the best."

The Denver Broncos improved to 7-2 with their fifth consecutive win as Bo Nix threw for 237 yards and two touchdowns in a 26-21 triumph at Carolina.

San Francisco improved to an NFL-best 7-1 with a 38-17 home victory over the Las Vegas Raiders as Brock Purdy threw for two touchdowns and ran for another.

The host Chicago Bears reached 7-2 with their fourth consecutive victory, edging Tampa Bay 27-24 on a 38-yard Cairo Santos field goal on the final play.

Caleb Williams threw for 279 yards and two touchdowns but also a career-high four interceptions. The Buccaneers scored off a fumble recovery to level the game with 2:51 remaining but Santos salvaged victory for Chicago.

Green Bay's Jordan Love threw for 372 yards and three touchdowns and ran for another score to spark the Packers (6-3) to victory 45-27 at New England.

Dak Prescott threw for 335 yards and two touchdowns while Javonte Williams ran for 101 yards and the deciding touchdown with 68 seconds remaining as Dallas won 27-23 at Indianapolis.

New Orleans edged visiting Cleveland 23-22 in overtime on Tyler Shough's 15-yard touchdown pass to Juwan Johnson. Cleveland's Shedeur Sanders tossed a 39-yard touchdown pass to Harold Fannin but a two-point conversion pass to win the game failed.

Matthew Stafford threw a seven-yard touchdown pass to Puka Nacua for the winning points in the Los Angeles Rams' 20-13 victory at Washington. Nacua caught 14 passes for 150 yards.

Jahmyr Gibbs ran for 74 yards and the only touchdown in Detroit's 19-9 victory at Miami, the Lions improving to 6-2.

Dominic Zvada kicked four field goals to lift the New York Giants over host Philadelphia 19-11, the seventh straight Eagles defeat.

Houston's CJ Stroud threw for 384 yards and five touchdowns as the Texans routed the winless Los Angeles Chargers 44-22.

AJ Barner caught a touchdown pass and ran for another touchdown in Seattle's 17-3 home triumph over Arizona.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Minnesota Vikings are adding to their receiving corps ahead of Monday night's matchup against the Buffalo Bills. Minnesota is signing former Pro Bowl receiver Odell Beckham Jr. to the 53-man roster, according to The Ringer.

Minnesota signed Beckham to its practice squad on Oct. 7, roughly a week after he was released by the New York Giants. Beckham was targeted just once in three games with the Giants prior to his release.

Beckham, who turned 34 on Nov. 5, made the Giants' initial 53-man roster after he missed the entire 2025 season. He played in nine games for the Dolphins in 2024 before being released in mid-December.

Beckham had plenty of early success in the NFL with the Giants. He was named to the Pro Bowl during each of his first three seasons. Beckham later had a 1,000-yard season with the Browns (in 2019) and helped the Rams win the Super Bowl at the end of the 2021 season.

During the Rams' Super Bowl win over the Bengals, Beckham had an early touchdown before he sustained an injury that sidelined him for the entire 2022 season. Beckham hasn't been the same player since that injury.

#2479. Mets legend Jerry Koosman dies at 83: Pitcher helped New York win 1969 World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Mets team Hall of Famer and two-time All-Star Jerry Koosman died Sunday morning in Osceola, Wisconsin, the team announced. He was 83. The Mets say Koosman battled multiple illnesses before his death.

"Kooz was one of the greatest pitchers in team history and a beloved member of the Mets family," Mets owners Alex and Steve Cohen said in a statement. "The 1969 Miracle Mets were filled with heroes, and the special southpaw from Appleton, Minnesota, was central to their success. He was a fierce competitor on the field, and respected teammate in the clubhouse. His legendary performance in the World Series helped the Mets secure their first Championship in team history. On behalf of the entire Mets organization, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Jerry's family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him."

The Mets discovered Koosman while he was pitching for the United States Army and signed him to a contract in August 1964. He made his MLB debut in April 1967 and moved into the rotation full-time the next season. Koosman threw 263 ⅔ innings with a 2.08 ERA as a rookie in 1968, which earned him an All-Star Game selection and MVP votes, and a second-place finish in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Hall of Famer Johnny Bench.

In 1969, Koosman was again an All-Star, throwing 241 innings with a 2.28 ERA. He was New York's No. 2 starter in the postseason between Hall of Famers Tom Seaver and Nolan Ryan. Koosman made two starts for the Miracle Mets in the World Series, including the Game 5 clincher against the Baltimore Orioles. He allowed three runs in the complete game win and recorded all but one possible out in his two World Series starts.

From 1968-76, Koosman was simply one of the best pitchers in the game, pitching to a 2.94 ERA and averaging 223 innings per season. The Mets traded him to the Minnesota Twins for Jesse Orosco in December 1978 and Koosman finished his career with stints for the Twins (1979-81), Chicago White Sox (1981-83), and Philadelphia Phillies (1984-85).

Koosman retired following the 1985 season with a 222-209 record and a 3.36 ERA that is 39th among AL/NL pitchers with at least 3,500 career innings. He ranks 35th all-time in strikeouts (2,556), 40th all-time in starts (527), 48th all-time in innings (3,839 ⅓), and 77th all-time in pitching WAR (57.0). Koosman went to two All-Star Games and finished second to Randy Jones in the 1976 Cy Young voting.

The Mets inducted Koosman into their Hall of Fame in 1989 and retired his No. 36 in 2021. His 140 wins are the most in franchise history among left-handers and third in team history overall, behind Seaver (198) and Dwight Gooden (157). Koosman is second in Mets history in innings (behind Seaver) and third in strikeouts (behind Seaver and Gooden).

Koosman fell off the Baseball Writers Association of America's Hall of Fame ballot in 1991, his first year of eligibility.

#2477. Caleb Williams' suboptimal SNF performance might have doomed his MVP hopes

CHICAGO — It was always going to be tough for Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams to be the NFL MVP this season.

He missed three games with a hamstring injury while Josh Allen, Joe Burrow and Brock Purdy have been dealing all season. But after Williams' followed his clinical performance against the Seattle Seahawks on Monday, Nov. 2 — 24 of 34 for 247 yards and a touchdown with no interceptions — with a blistering start against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday, Nov. 8, it looked as if he could at least put himself in the conversation.

And then his slim hopes imploded with three picks in nine plays. That's right. Any chance, however slim, Williams had of challenging the current favorites for MVP was over by halftime.

The guy who'd had one interception in his first five games this season suddenly had three in one quarter. To put a finer point on it, Williams had thrown one interception in his first 175 pass attempts this year. He had three in seven attempts during the second quarter, with the first two coming on back-to-back attempts.

And he wasn't done! Williams threw a fourth interception late in the third quarter.

It's the first four-interception game of his NFL career. Scratch that. It's the first four-interception game he's had in the NFL or college. He threw three picks in last year's NFC divisional-round loss to the Los Angeles Rams, and had three in a loss to Notre Dame during his last season at USC.

Williams had never thrown more than two picks in a regular-season NFL game. And the only multi-interception games he's had were way back in the first month of his rookie season, before Bears coach and quarterback whisperer Ben Johnson arrived.

So, no. Williams is not going to be crowned the NFL's best player this season. He might not even be the best player in his own division, what with the way Jordan Love has been playing of late.

The only redeeming factor of Williams' terrible, horrible, no good, very bad day? The Bears still won, 27-24, because the Bucs were somehow even worse! Hard to believe, I know. Baker Mayfield had a pair of interceptions of his own and was sacked four times.

The most surprising thing of all this is Williams seemed poised to have a big day. A big, big, big day. Tampa Bay has been stifling against the run this season, coming into the game allowing just 80 yards rushing. And Williams came out firing, connecting on four of his first five attempts, including a 9-yard pass to Rome Odunze to give the Bears a 7-0 lead on the first possession of the game.

Follow USA TODAY Sports columnist Nancy Armour on social media @nrarmour.

Here are the game's best defenders in 2026 according to Statcast's Fielding Runs Value, an all-encompassing metric that factors in range and arm, as well as blocking and framing for catchers:

Gold Gloves have be awarded since 1957 and are given to the best defensive player at each position in each league. That first year was one MLB-wide honor at each position. In 1958, Gold Gloves were split into AL and NL. Also, it used to be three outfielders per league regardless of exact position. Now the outfield spots are broken down into left field, center field, and right field.

Winners are determined through manager/coach voting (75%) and a statistical component (25%). Team employees can not vote for their own players.

While MLB announced "finalists" for each Gold Glove a few weeks back, remember that the voting was already complete and those finalists were simply the top three vote-getters at each position. #2473. NBA Bracketology: Projecting the full 20-team postseason field as Knicks, Thunder take steps back

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA comes at you fast. One moment the Knicks are riding high off their first championship in 53 years, the next they're off to a sluggish start and scrambling to recover from losing their first three games. The Thunder went into the season rightly hailed as one of the deepest teams in the NBA — then had that assumption tested in harsh fashion after sustaining injuries to three of their five starters, with Jalen Williams (ankle and fibula) and Cason Wallace (shoulder) expected to miss most, if not all, of the season, and Chet Holmgren (knee) out at least two months.

While OKC suffered the most brutal blows on the injury front, the Thunder are hardly alone there. Several big name stars have already gone down and missed multiple games, among them Anthony Edwards (knee), Kawhi Leonard (knee), Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring), Jalen Duren (hamstring), Paolo Banchero (ankle), Jaren Jackson Jr (knee) and Ja Morant (hamstring).

The net effect is that an NBA season that was already expected to be competitive and wide open — particularly in the East, where the conference is as deep as it's been in recent memory — has been thrown into flux. While the Spurs and Thunder remain the betting favorites to win it all, the Sixers, Knicks, Celtics, Rockets, Raptors and Timberwolves are bunched up right behind them, with the Nuggets, Pistons, Cavaliers, Lakers and Blazers not far behind.

In the actual standings, the new-look Sixers have won seven of their first eight and are perched atop the Eastern Conference, while the surprising Memphis Grizzlies got out to a hot start in the West and were the last team in the league to lose their first game after getting upended by the Pelicans in overtime at home on Monday night. Meanwhile, Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Heat are under .500 and still trying to figure it out, while the Wolves and Warriors are just two teams out of several trying to stay afloat until key members of their respective teams return to the floor.

Various prediction models have differing opinions on what all this means in the long run. Those forecasts vary wildly, with one favoring the Raptors to come out of the East and another giving four other teams a better shot to win the conference than Toronto.

Predicting how all this will shake out in the end is difficult at best and folly at worst — so naturally that's exactly what we'll try to do over the course of the season.

This is our first installment of semi-regular NBA seeding predictions -- the NBA version of Bracketology -- where we'll give our best guess on where teams will be slotted once the playoffs roll around. The methodology is super scientific: watch a lot of basketball, consult with the mountain of stats and data available, and then eyeball it. Your mileage may vary.

Despite Duren playing all of 38 minutes this season, the Pistons have reminded everyone why they were the top seed in the East last season and have designs on something similar again this year. Detroit has proven to be a quality regular-season team, but the Pistons are still in desperate need of more shot creators and scoring to help ease the burden on Cade Cunningham. Their front office has work to do to level up the roster and avoid another disappointing postseason.

After what could charitably be called a tumultuous offseason, the Celtics once again look like a competitive, competent organization (apart from their struggles in Houston on Monday in the second night of a back-to-back) that figures to be a tough out in the East. Jayson Tatum is playing well enough to openly wonder "why not me?" when it comes to the MVP conversation, while Paul George's numbers to start the season look a lot more like the PG we saw in his final campaign with the Clippers rather than (mercifully for him and Boston) the lackluster version who was only intermittently available during his time in Philadelphia.

There were questions about the new-look Sixers going into the season, mainly how four big-name stars in the starting lineup would co-exist. The answer to date is that they've figured out ways to win when things have sometimes looked bleak. The Sixers lead the league in clutch victories, with six of their seven wins coming in games decided by five points or fewer with under five minutes to go. More surprising: they're top five in defensive rating and have allowed the second fewest points per game.

On paper, the Knicks have the best starting five in the NBA. That hasn't changed. Even though they didn't start the season looking like the dominant version of themselves that ripped through the playoffs en route to a title, the talent in New York remains undeniable.

The Raptors were a good defensive team last year and figure to be so again, but how far Toronto goes this season will be directly tied to Kawhi's availability — something that has been largely unknowable for much of the last decade of Leonard's career. As for the Cavaliers, their starting five is among the best in the league. After that, the roster gets thin and the questions begin to mount for Kenny Atkinson and the analytics team.

Maybe this is disrespecting the Hawks by lumping them with three teams that hardly inspire confidence, but the East feels like it has a solid six and then a pretty squishy bunch jockeying for play-in positioning. Miami fans won't like being in this group either — even though members of the Heat overreacted to their ugly start just like the rest of us and wondered aloud about the floor spacing and fit between Giannis and Bam Adebayo. Banchero is once again hurt in Orlando, but even when he's healthy, he and Franz Wagner (who is still searching for his elusive 3-point shot) have achieved exactly nothing together. The Wizards have been surprisingly plucky to begin the season, but if you're skeptical about Trae Young and Anthony Davis being on the floor enough to actually influence their record and help them sneak into the play-in, you aren't alone. Feel free to swap out the Hornets for one of these last-chance slots; Charlotte has been without the services of Kon Knueppel (hamstring) thus far and would undoubtedly benefit from his return.

Not pictured: the Pacers, who will be going nowhere fast if Haliburton and Ivica Zubac (ankle) don't get back on the floor sooner than later and stay there.

The Spurs are the biggest beneficiaries of the league-wide injury virus that has yet to infect them. The defending Western Conference champs are healthy, which is more than most teams can say. They still need to figure out the crowded and sometimes clunky backcourt fit between De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper, but as long as Victor Wembanyama is available, the West is once again theirs for the taking.

The Rockets were sorely in need of guard play last season after Fred VanVleet missed the season with a knee injury. He's back, and Houston has looked stout at both ends of the floor to begin the season (including Monday evening's comfortable home win over the Celtics). But is FVV's return enough to boost the Rockets and propel them to a deep postseason run, or does Houston need to make a move in a conference that is suddenly up for grabs outside of San Antonio? There will be endless rumors between now and the trade deadline about how the Rockets could use someone like Kyrie Irving — which does not mean the Mavericks will be keen on moving him.

If there's any team that could withstand losing three of its five starters for a significant chunk of the season, it's OKC. Sam Presti has done a masterful job making the Thunder into the deepest team in the league, but this represents the biggest challenge OKC has faced since developing into a perennial contender. How much weight can Shai Gilgeous-Alexander be reasonably expected to carry, and will guys like Ajay Mitchell, Isaiah Hartenstein, Alex Caruso, Jared McCain, and rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz be able to fill the void created in the absence of Williams, Wallace and Holmgren?

Luka Dončić is off to a scorching start, leads the league in scoring and has played better defense at times (and doesn't mind saying so himself), though even JJ Redick has openly questioned the roster and what the ancillary parts can be reasonably trusted with on a nightly basis. The Nuggets are once again thin after the starting five and are heavily reliant on Nikola Jokić and Jamal Murray. And through the first five games, the Blazers boasted the third-best point differential in the league — but also lost Morant to a hamstring injury that will keep him out of the lineup for a while. At least it's Dame Time in Portland again.

There were those of us who doubted the fit with Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball and wondered whether the duo could make the Wolves into contenders — and that was before the team announced that Edwards would undergo an unexpected in-season knee surgery. That's asking Ball to do a lot in his absence. Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has played well and talked even better, but Golden State is still painfully thin while waiting for Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody to return from knee injuries (to say nothing of Kristaps Porzingis, whose status remains a mystery). Kyrie's name has been unsurprisingly floated in various trade rumors, but the Mavericks just might be competitive enough to entertain keeping him around. After moving on from Desmond Bane, Jaren Jackson Jr and Morant, the Grizzlies were supposed to be rebooting the franchise around rookie Cam Boozer. Memphis benefited mightily from a paper-thin schedule to start with wins over the Jazz (twice), Kings (twice), Warriors and Blazers before the Pelicans finally handed them their first L. It only gets harder from here — but even qualifying for the play-in would represent a successful season in Memphis.

LeBron James had his best game yet for the Philadelphia 76ers, who bounced back with a 127-121 win in Chicago on Sunday over a Bulls side that has now lost seven straight NBA games.

Veteran superstar James scored 22 points -- his highest tally since joining the Sixers this summer -- in a return to form after a paltry eight points in Friday's disappointing loss to Cleveland.

James also had five assists while Jaylen Brown top-scored with 29, Tyrese Maxey poured in 27 and Joel Embiid pulled down 10 rebounds.

The star-studded Sixers have lost just twice so far this season, for their best start after 11 games since 2000.

Philadelphia grabbed the lead early in the second quarter and never trailed from there, though a resilient Chicago pulled within two points in the closing stages.

"We have a lot of guys that's been in situations, late-game situations, and we have a 'no panic' button," said James.

"We understand that we got to get stops on this end, but if teams make a run, we understand how to be calm on the other end as well."

The Bulls remain second-bottom of the Eastern Conference, ahead of only the Milwaukee Bucks -- the only team Chicago has beaten so far this campaign.

They were without shooting guard Norman Powell, their second-leading scorer this season, who was placed on the injury report hours before tip-off with back discomfort.

But Josh Giddey provided some hope with a double-double including 19 points and 15 assists.

Meanwhile, James' former Los Angeles Lakers team overcame the absence of red-hot talisman Luka Doncic to beat the Detroit Pistons 121-116, and also move to 9-2.

Doncic, who has been averaging more than 40 points per game this season, was left out with lower back tightness, the team announced.

Austin Reaves stepped up, scoring 43 points, including two calm free throws in the final seconds to take the game beyond Detroit's reach.

The Lakers never trailed but had to fight hard to retain a razor-thin lead for most of the fourth quarter.

Daniss Jenkins led the Pistons' comeback attempt from the bench with 31 points, while Kevin Huerter added 24.

Minnesota extended its fine start with a 115-100 win over struggling Utah. It was the Timberwolves' fourth straight win despite losing Anthony Edwards to injury.

The Bucks suffered another loss, falling 117-97 to the Celtics, who rallied from an early 14-point deficit, while Dallas thumped Brooklyn 130-93.

Giannis Antetokounmpo top-scored for Miami in a 114-108 win at Sacramento with 29 points and 14 rebounds, while the Los Angeles Clippers grabbed a rare win, defeating New Orleans 139-123.

The Charlotte Hornets announced that forward Kon Knueppel will miss at least four weeks with a left hamstring strain, while guard Dennis Schroder is out for at least two weeks with the same injury.

I'm done. No more. Enough is enough. I have doubted the Brewers far too many times and I decided in early August to never do it again. I started picking them to win the World Series every chance I got. I was finally right.

Every time they traded away someone good (the latest being Freddy Peralta last offseason), I thought, "OK, now is when it finally catches up with them." Only it never does. I thought they needed Tarik Skubal, both to reinforce their rotation and also to keep him away from the Dodgers. It didn't matter. They beat him and swept the Dodgers in the NLCS.

They develop young stars better than anyone. There's another one coming in Jesús Made, but there's no reason for Brewers fans to dream about the future when the present is World Series champions.

Jackson Chourio is becoming a superstar, Jacob Misiorowski is going to win the National League Cy Young and Christian Yelich is a former MVP, but it isn't really about the big names with this group. It's everything. It's the entire team making this train run, working as a cohesive unit. It's Robert Gasser going out and dealing in Game 3 after starting the season in the minors. It's Jake Bauers winning NLCS MVP not too long after he was ready to retire from baseball. It's Aaron Ashby putting up one of the greatest reliever performances in playoff history. It's Sal Frelick hitting a game-tying bomb. It's Cooper Pratt's coming-out party in the World Series. And on and on and on we could go.

Milwaukee is the best organization in baseball now, supplanting the former two-time defending champion Dodgers.

#2467. Clippers beat Pelicans to end 7-game losing streak

INGLEWOOD, Calif. (AP) — Darius Garland had 24 points and 10 assists, Brook Lopez added 20 points and the Los Angeles Clippers ended a seven-game losing streak with a 139-123 victory over the New Orleans Pelicans on Sunday night.

Gradey Dick and rookie Keaton Wagler each scored 15 points and Rui Hachimura added 14 as the Clippers won for the first time since getting past the Sacramento Kings in the season opener.

The Clippers went on a 15-6 run to open the fourth quarter to take control with a 117-101 lead and finished off the victory after failing to hold on to double-digit fourth-quarter leads in their previous two games.

Trey Murphy III scored 26 points, while Zion Williamson and Jeremiah Fears each added 25 as the Pelicans lost their second consecutive game following a four-game winning streak. Saddiq Bey had 13 points for New Orleans, which was playing the opener of a two-game California trip.

The Pelicans shot 50.6% from the floor while getting held to 52 points in the paint after entering the with 61.6 per game in that department to lead the NBA.

The Clippers took a 124-107 lead with 4:56 remaining on three free throws from Garland and cruised to the victory from there with a season high in points. Los Angeles shot a season-best 54.8% from the floor.

The Clippers led 67-60 at halftime after shooting 52.3% from the floor and getting 14 points from Garland, while Williamson had 17 points for the Pelicans. New Orleans opened the second half on an 18-10 run to take their first lead since the opening minute at 78-77.

Los Angeles was without center Isaiah Jackson (groin), as well as former Pelicans star Brandon Ingram (heel), who is close to his debut for his new team.

Pelicans: At Golden State on Monday night.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2464. Tarik Skubal landing spots: Predicting new home for two-time Cy Young winner, the offseason's best free agent

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Arguably the best pitcher in baseball is up for grabs this winter. Tarik Skubal is a free agent for the 2026-27 MLB offseason, easily the top available on the market, and every team should be trying to earn his services. But will they? Almost certainly not.

The 29-year-old southpaw spent the first six years of his major-league career with the Detroit Tigers before being traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers at the 2026 deadline. He won back-to-back Cy Young awards in 2024 and 2025 and earned MVP votes in both seasons. He's likely to become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history both in total value and AAV.

Of course, the giant flashing sign floating above all of this is the expiring CBA, which will run out at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1, after which the owners are expected to lock out the players until a new deal is reached. Over the summer, the league proposed limiting free agency contracts, an offer that the players' union quickly disavowed, and the owners' demand for a salary cap is the underlying throughline of every negotiation. Perhaps that means Skubal will rush to sign on the dotted line before new rules are in place. Perhaps that means teams will wait out the negotiations until they know how much they have to spend -- and how they'll be punished if they do so.

Regardless, CBS Sports' MLB experts, three people who are very much not involved in contract negotiations, have gathered to predict where Skubal lands by the time Opening Day rolls around.

Mike Axisa: I'll go off the board a bit and say the Padres. The new ownership group didn't pay $3.9 billion for the franchise only to cheap out in their first offseason. They're moneyed and motivated, and that's usually enough to land the top free agents. It should appeal to Skubal too. The Padres are in the postseason most years, they play in a great (and largely pitcher-friendly) ballpark, and it's San Diego. How can you not love San Diego? Skubal to the Padres because the new owners want to make a big splash in their first offseason. That's my prediction.

Dayn Perry: I'll say the Mets top all offers by a margin sufficient to overcome their lack of appeal compared to the usual suspects (meaning, mostly, the Dodgers). They definitely need a stabilizing force in the rotation outside of Nolan McLean, and they also need a vibes shift after the deeply disappointing 2026 campaign. Landing the biggest fish of all on the market would provide all that and meet a clear need. The Mets will already be rebound candidates in 2027, and signing the likes of Skubal would position them as contenders. Obviously, the structure of the next CBA has bearing here, but maybe this all comes together before the lockout shuts it all down for an indeterminate period of time.

Matt Snyder: I'll go with the easy and obvious answer and say the Dodgers. #2458. Ty Jerome is on a Linsanity-esque run, but here's why his MVP-level scoring isn't that big of a surprise

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Memphis Grizzlies finally lost a game on Monday night, their first of the year. But, of course, Ty Jerome was still the story. The Grizzlies point guard, who has gone full Linsanity Mode to start the season, rattled off 40 points on 64% shooting against the Pelicans. He made five of his six 3-pointers. He made seven of his eight free throws.

With the Grizzlies trailing 124-115 at the 1:43 mark, Jerome engineered a personal 9-0 run to close regulation and send the game to overtime.

TY JEROME HEATER TO FORCE OT!!! pic.twitter.com/kmet2W6esv

Less than two weeks removed from opening night (when Jerome put 45 on the Jazz), it's obviously too early to have a real MVP discussion. But, if we could, Jerome would be in it. The league's sixth-leading scorer, he's now averaging 28.3 points per game on 50/42/88 shooting splits.

People are wondering: how is this possible? Wasn't this guy a G League player? Yes, he was. But that was five years ago, and if you've been paying attention, you know he's been making consistent leaps as he has earned more and more opportunities. It's not to say anyone could've seen this kind of scoring boom coming, but there were signs.

Agfter bumping around with the Suns, Thunder and Warriors through the first four years of his career, Jerome, who had played well with whatever time he got specifically in OKC and Golden State, broke out with the Cavs during the 2024-25 season. He averaged 12.5 PPG on 51/44 shooting splits, finished third in Sixth Man of the Year voting, and became a legit go-to scorer in the playoffs.

In Clevaland's first-round sweep over the Heat, Jerome averaged over 16 PPG, making 10 of his 20 3-pointers and shooting 51% overall. In Game 1, he scored 16 of his 28 points on 6-of-7 shooting in the fourth quarter.

Look deeper at that season, and you'll see that Jerome was an All-Star-level scorer relative to his playing time, averaging 22.7 points per 36 minutes. That was a better mark that Jamal Murray, Tyrese Haliburton and Jimmy Butler, among many others. The only reason he wasn't a 20 PPG scorer was he only played 19.9 minutes per night on a Cleveland team that had Donovan Mitchell and Darius Garland ahead of him.

The Grizzlies saw this, and in the summer of 2025 signed Jerome to a three-year, $28 million contract that now looks like the biggest non-rookie bargain in the league. He only played in 15 games last season, but once again he was a per-minute monster.

After missing the first three-plus months to a calf strain, Jerome scored 20 points in 20 minutes in his Grizzlies debut, and over the following six weeks he averaged 0.87 points per minute played, the same mark as Kawhi Leonard and fourth-best in the league among players who logged at least 10 games.

The evidence was clear: If Jerome is on the court, he's going to score. It's just a matter of playing time. So far this season, he's playing 30 minutes per night, and is currently scoring 0.91 points in each of those minutes. That registers as the fourth-best mark in the league among players who have played at least 100 minutes.

It's not to say we should've seen an MVP-level start coming for Jerome, but at the same time this scoring wave he's currently riding didn't come out of nowhere. The signs trace back to Cleveland. As his minutes, and usage, have gone up, so too has his scoring. He is simply playing more minutes now with a 31.3% usage rate equal to Jalen Brunson.

Again, that's not to say Jerome is a superstar. But don't be thrown off by his underdog story or his lack of NBA athleticism. He's extraordinarily skilled and always has been. He's a world-class shooter, both off the catch and dribble, near and far. Going back to Cleveland, he has consistently ranked north of the 90th percentile as both a pick-and-roll and isolation scorer, per Synergy. What he's doing to start this season probably won't continue, but it also didn't come out of nowhere.

#2457. Contemporary Baseball Era Committee unveils eight Hall of Fame candidates: Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The National Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown on Monday announced eight candidates for election on the 2027 Contemporary Baseball Era Committee ballot. The non-player ballot includes four former managers and four former executives: Sandy Alderson, Dusty Baker, Bruce Bochy, Joe Maddon, Lou Piniella, Brian Sabean, Ted Turner, and Bill White.

The non-player ballot includes managers, executives, and umpires. On an alternating basis, the Era Committee also evaluates a ballot consisting of former players. As for the qualifications and criteria, the Hall of Fame describes it thus:

"The eight Contemporary Baseball Era finalists were selected by the BBWAA-appointed Historical Overview Committee from all eligible candidates among managers, umpires and executives whose most significant career impact was realized since 1980. Eligible candidates include managers and umpires with 10 or more major league seasons and retired for at least five years (candidates who are 65 years or older are eligible six months following retirement); and executives retired for at least five years (active executives 70 years or older are eligible for consideration regardless of the position they hold in an organization and regardless of whether their body of work has been completed). All candidates must not be on Baseball's Ineligible List."

As for those figures on the Era Committee ballot for 2027, here's a quick rundown:

Alderson built a powerhouse and won a World Series as general manager of the Oakland A's. He later earned multiple playoff berths and a pennant as GM of the New York Mets.

One of the winningest managers of all time, Baker guided five different clubs to the playoffs and won three pennants and a World Series. His success in the dugout came after a long and distinguished playing career as an MLB outfielder.

Bochy as a manager led three different clubs to the postseason and is one of just six managers ever to win at least four World Series. Three of Bochy's rings came with the San Francisco Giants, and the final one came with the Texas Rangers in 2023.

Maddon won more than 1,300 games as a manager for three different franchises. He also won a pennant as manager of the Tampa Bay Rays, and in 2016, he led the Chicago Cubs to their first World Series title in more than a century.

After an 18-year playing career, Piniella racked up more than 1,800 wins as a big-league manager. He led three different clubs to the playoffs, won a World Series as manager of the 1990 Cincinnati Reds, and in 2001 helmed the Seattle Mariners to a record 116 wins during the regular season.

After filling a key role in the New York Yankees front office, Sabean joined the Giants as their general manager. Under his guidance, the Giants won the World Series in 2010, 2012, and 2014.

The only posthumous candidate on the ballot, Turner owned the Atlanta Braves for two decades. Along the way, he innovated the distribution of televised baseball games and oversaw a dynasty. Under Turner's stewardship, the Braves claimed 14 straight division titles and won the World Series in 1995.

A five-time All-Star and Gold Glove first baseman as a player, White after his playing days were over served as president of the National League. White was also the first Black play-by-play broadcaster in MLB history, and his leadership of the NL made him the first Black president of a major sports league.

The results of the committee vote will be announced on MLB Network at 8 p.m. ET on Sunday, Dec. 6. As with the BBWAA ballot, a candidate must be named on at least 75% of ballots in order to earn election. A 16-member committee will vote on the candidates.

The more traditional BBWAA ballot, in which candidates are voted on by writers and other media members, will be revealed on Nov. 16. Results of the 2027 BBWAA ballot will be announced in January, at which point we'll know the full Hall of Fame class for 2027.

Adam Jahns: It was ugly. Very, very ugly. But it's a win. The Bears looked like a team dealing with a bunch of injuries coming off a short week and an exhausting, emotional win over the defending Super Bowl champions on the road. #2454. NBA Power Rankings: Warriors fly into top 10 with rejuvenated Stephen Curry, 76ers pushing for top spot

After the Warriors' win over Phoenix on Monday, their fifth straight (something they never managed last season), Stephen Curry was asked what about this year's squad feels different from the one that finished with 37 wins a year ago.

"I mean, Yax," Curry laughed, stating the obvious when it comes to the historic start of Warriors' rookie Yaxel Lendeborg. "BP [Brandin Podziemski] taking another step forward. B-Will [Brandon Williams] has been great for us off the bench, giving us something we haven't had in a while. We've had some individual production that's been pretty cool, some standout guys who've made their presence felt night after night.

"But I think collectively," Curry continued, "we're probably a little bit more prepared on the details of what we're trying to do, and not just taking for granted that you can just play like the Warriors of old and expect good things to happen."

Curry didn't elaborate on these "details" on which the Warriors are more focused this season, but it looks about the same on the statistical surface. They're playing at the same pace. Making the same amount of 3s. They're still a high-turnover offense. They remain small, collectively old and not particularly athletic. They own a nearly identical 114-ish defensive rating, which at the moment has them ranked as a bottom-10 unit. Their spot-up, pick-and-roll, transition and isolation frequencies are all pretty much the same, per Synergy.

Which is to say, the Warriors are, in fact, playing like the Warriors. They look so good, that they've jumped 15 spots this week into the top 10 of our weekly NBA Power Rankings. Let's break down three reasons why.

Anyone who says they can see slippage in Curry's game must be looking through one hell of a high-powered microscope. He's scoring more than a point a minute (30 PPG in 28.8 MPG). The only other player doing that, with at least 100 minutes played, is Luka Dončić.

Get this: According to Cleaning the Glass, the 137.4 points that Curry is currently scoring per 100 shot attempts registers as a career high. He's taking more than 10 3-pointers a night and connecting at a 43% clip. On Monday, he finally missed a free throw after making 51 straight to start the year.

So yeah, Curry is still Curry. The difference is, he's got a real co-star again (remember, this team was tracking toward a conference finals trip when Jimmy Butler first came over) in the form a 24-year-old rookie.

Even knowing Curry's greatness, just about everyone pegged Golden State as a lottery team this year. They may still end up there, but at the moment Lendeborg has completely revived a team that we had all left for dead. He's the only rookie in history other than Larry Bird to post at least 100 points, 40 rebounds and 20 assists through his first five games. He's just the third player in Warriors history to average north of 20 PPG (22.3) over his first seven games of his career, joining Wilt Chamberlain and Rick Barry. In the win over the Clippers on Sunday, he became the fourth rookie in history log a game with at least 37 points and five assists on 85% true shooting.

Lendeborg is tracking toward Rookie of the Year and honest All-Star consideration. He has given the Warriors a legit first option without Curry on the court, and, in tandem, he massively eases Curry's burden as a creator. The guy is already a pick-and-roll machine and, at the moment, the most efficient isolation scorer in the league.

For some reason Podziemski has become a punching bag for a lot of Warriors fans, but he's been a winning player from day one (just go look at his on/off splits dating back to his rookie year). With Butler out, and until Lendeborg came along, Podziemski was the only Warrior other than Curry who could generate real paint pressure.

This season, Podziemski is putting it all together to the tune of a career-high 17 points, five assists and five boards per game. Once again, the splits tell the tale: The Warriors have outscored opponents by 50 points with Podziemski on the floor so far this year, by far the team high.

Suddenly the Warriors have three to four guys on any given night who can break a defense down, and with that you're seeing these support-staff guys like Georges Niang, Gui Santos, De'Anthony Melton, Gary Payton II, Will Richard, Al Horford, and even Charles Bassey (who has gone from taking DNPs to putting up 25 points and 18 boards over the last two games) to ride shotgun on a top-five offense.

#2453. Eight MLB players tagged with $23.15M qualifying offer: Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Jake Bauers, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight MLB free agents were extended a one-year, $23.15 million contract offer on Monday that, if declined, could fetch their old teams draft-pick compensation. That group includes Randy Arozarena and Seiya Suzuki.

This is one of the smallest groups of qualifying offers ever. Only six players got one in 2020. There were 13 last offseason, and we've seen as many as 20. From 2012 to 2025, 157 qualifying offers were made and only 18 accepted, including a record four last year.

Each offseason, certain free agents are eligible for the qualifying offer (QO). Those eligible free agents have never before received the QO and who spent the prior season with only one team (in other words, players traded during the season cannot receive the QO). The QO is set as the average of the top 125 salaries for a given year, and for the 2026-27 offseason it's a record $23.15 million.

Eligible players who accept the QO will play the 2027 season under that salary for their 2026 team, while those who turn it down become free agents, albeit with the QO compensation attached. That attachment means that the free agent's former team is entitled to an additional draft pick. The position of that draft pick depends upon the team's status when it comes to the luxury tax and revenue-sharing debits or credits.

On the other side, a team that signs a free agent with a QO attached is penalized with the loss of a draft pick, depending again upon the signing team's classification when it comes to the luxury tax and revenue sharing.

Most QO decisions are obvious. Premium free agents receive one without much thought, just as the much less coveted class of free agents do not. It's in the middle ground that interesting decisions lie -- first on the club side and then, if offered, on the player side. That's even more the case this year, when the expiring CBA and negotiations toward a new one have already included talk of a salary cap and restrictions on free agent contracts.

Players presented with a QO this offseason will have until 4 p.m. ET on Nov. 17 to accept or reject the offer.

Below you'll find a rundown of the eight players who received a QO. Do note the players are listed in order of their free agent ranking.

One of the top relievers in baseball over the last three seasons, Morejón gains attractiveness on the open market due to having an effective four-pitch arsenal. That means it's possible he and the team he signs with will want him to convert to a starting pitcher. He could stay in relief, too, where it's likely he'd continue to dominate. A path needs to be chosen, but this guy is a special talent.

Rogers was traded to the Orioles in 2024 and struggled to the point that he needed a trip to the minors. Once he returned in 2025, he was outstanding, pitching to a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts. He struggled to start last season, but made some adjustments and had a 2.90 ERA in his last 20 starts. He's the fallback option to Tarik Skubal, who wasn't eligible for a qualifying offer after a midseason trade.

The power-speed threat posted his sixth straight 20-20 season in 2026 along with an excellent .381 on-base percentage and career-best 5.7 WAR. He's hitting free agency at the right time, though he heads to his age-32 season with sustainability questions, not to mention a few under-the-hood reasons to worry about things going downhill moving forward. Still, it's a weak class for big bats and he'll get paid.

Thanks in large part to huge improvements on defense, Suzuki posted a career-high 5.1 WAR in 2026. His batting average and slugging percentage were right in line with his established career marks and he improved his walk rate to rock a higher OBP. The best path forward is probably to ignore the defensive gains and realize there's a high floor here with the bat for another several years.

There were trade rumors about Jeffers last July, but the Twins hung around in the playoff race and ended up being buyers. Injury limited Jeffers to just 92 games, but on a rate basis he's been a very good hitting catcher for four years, along with being a quality backstop as well.

The NLCS MVP and World Series champion is coming off a career year at the plate. He had a 140 OPS+ and 3.3 WAR in 144 games and 578 plate appearances, serving as the two-hole hitter for the Brewers throughout the playoffs. He heads to his age-31 season, and this might well be the opportunity of his lifetime for one huge payday.

Lowe just posted a career-high 5.4 WAR in 150 games in his first season with the Pirates, topping 30 home runs for the third time in his career, and he averages 35 homers per 162 games. Are the defensive gains real or a one-year outlier? Will his struggles against lefties prevent a long-term deal?

While there has been some inconsistency (he was brutal for some of 2024, for example), Bednar is coming off a big 2026 season. He was one of the best closers in baseball and showed with the Yankees he can handle a high-profile closing job. He also has a good playoff track record. There isn't much of a top-level closer market in free agency, so he's surely turning this down.

Week 9 is underway across the NFL, but looming over all the on-field action is what's happening behind the scenes ahead of Tuesday's trade deadline. However, it doesn't sound like Cousins is going to wear a new uniform once Week 10 rolls around.

The Raiders have not received any trade calls this weekend regarding Cousins, according to ESPN. Moreover, Las Vegas is reportedly not interested in dealing him either. They want to stay the course with their plan to keep Cousins as their starter until they believe Mendoza is ready.

Entering Week 9, Cousins has 19 passing touchdowns, which is second in the NFL and only looking up to Joe Burrow in Cincinnati (20). He's also completing 63.6% of his passes with a 101.4 passer rating over his first eight starts. The Raiders enter Week 9 at 4-4 on the season and still within striking range of a wild card spot, which is likely why Las Vegas is apprehensive about moving Cousins.

While the team is currently holding firm, it will be interesting to see if that changes, particularly after Week 9. One team that has been linked to Cousins has been the Minnesota Vikings, whom he played for from 2018 to 2023. With Kyler Murray dealing with a Grade 2 hamstring injury, they do have a need at quarterback as they make a playoff push, entering Week 9 with a 6-1 record and in first place in the NFC North.

#2449. Pete Crow-Armstrong, Jacob Misiorowski, more named finalists for MVP, Cy Young and Rookie of the Year awards

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball, in conjunction with the Baseball Writers Association of America (BBWAA), has announced the finalists for the 2026 major awards: Most Valuable Player, Cy Young, Rookie of the Year, Reliever of the Year and Manager of the Year.

As a reminder, the voting was completed before the playoffs even started. In fact, ballots were due before the first pitch of the playoffs. That means these are regular-season awards. Further, there's no voting after finalists are announced or anything like that. The word "finalists" is kind of misleading, too. The ballots have already been tabulated and the league office is simply revealing the top three vote-getters for each award to create a buzz before the winners are announced.

Take note that the BBWAA has added a new award this season: Relief Pitcher of the Year for each league. MLB has been naming the Mariano Rivera American League Reliever of the Year and Trevor Hoffman National League Reliever of the Year, but this is the first time the BBWAA has added an award for a relief pitcher.

Monday, Nov. 9: Jackie Robinson Rookie of the Year Awards

Tuesday, Nov. 10: Manager of the Year Awards

Wednesday, Nov. 11: Relief Pitcher of the Year Awards

Thursday, Nov. 12: Most Valuable Player Awards

Yordan Alvarez, Astros: He stayed healthy for a full season and was every bit as good as we all thought he'd be. In 158 games, Alvarez had 34 doubles, 42 homers, 106 RBI, 105 runs and led the majors in all three slashes: .316/.432/.601 (190 OPS+). He also led the majors in walks and intentional walks.

Junior Caminero, Rays: At age 22, he played all 162 games, leading the Rays to the best AL record. He hit .276/.360/.524 (144 OPS+) with 42 home runs, 101 RBI and 100 runs, posting a 5.7 WAR. He's already made history, too, as the Rays had previously never had a player finish in the top five of MVP voting.

Bobby Witt Jr., Royals: This is now Witt's fourth straight season in the top seven and third straight season in the top four. He finished second in 2024. This season, he hit .281/.359/.441 (125 OPS+) with 33 doubles, 18 homers, 54 RBI, 94 runs, 45 steals and 6.7 WAR.

Dylan Cease, Blue Jays: In his first season after signing a big deal with the Jays, Cease was one of the few bright spots for the disappointing ballclub. He went 11-6 with a 2.40 ERA (184 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 239 strikeouts in 169 innings, finishing with 5.5 WAR. He was the All-Star Game starter.

Parker Messick, Guardians: In 32 starts, Messick was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings, helping the Guardians win the AL Central for the third straight season. Fun fact: Eight pitchers in history have won the Rookie of the Year and Cy Young. Fernando Valenzuela in 1981 is the only one to win both in the same year.

Cam Schlittler, Yankees: Fresh off a great half season and playoffs in 2025, Schlittler just kept impressing. In his age-25 season, he was 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP and 239 strikeouts in 193 ⅔ innings, holding the Yankees rotation together despite several key injuries. He led the AL in WAR and ERA.

Kevin McGonigle, Tigers: A first-round pick out of high school in 2023, McGonigle made the Tigers out of spring training and took the league by storm. He returned home to Philadelphia for the All-Star Game and finished with an AL-best 7.1 WAR. In 707 plate appearances, he hit .278/.376/.420 (126 OPS+) with 28 doubles, five triples, 18 home runs, 72 RBI, 97 runs and 12 steals, all the while playing good defense at both shortstop and third base.

Parker Messick, Guardians: The southpaw got his feet wet in 2025, but the workload was low enough that he maintained rookie status for 2026, during which he excelled. In 32 starts, Messick was 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings, helping the Guardians win the AL Central for the third straight season.

Payton Tolle, Red Sox: The 6-foot-6 lefty was a second-round pick in 2024 and debuted last season, though he didn't even work 20 innings and struggled. This time around, he was ready. In 26 starts, he was 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA (135 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.

Bryan Baker, Rays: After dabbling in relative obscurity for parts of five seasons, Baker broke out at age 31 this year. He led the majors with 41 saves while pitching to a 1.44 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 63 strikeouts in his 62 ⅓ innings for the best team in the AL.

Cade Smith, Guardians: Tied with Baker for the MLB lead in saves with 41, Smith was nails in his first full season as closer. He had a 1.95 ERA, 0.96 WHIP and 107 strikeouts in 74 innings for a playoff team.

Louis Varland, Blue Jays: In his fifth MLB season, Varland really found something and finished with a 1.27 ERA, 1.00 WHIP and 97 strikeouts in 78 innings. By late April, he was the Jays' closer, finishing 35 of 37 save chances.

Kevin Cash, Rays: The Rays missed the playoffs in 2024 and 2025 and returned to the Trop after hurricane damage left them without a home in '25. They went out and won 98 games and took one of the toughest divisions in baseball, finishing as the best team in the AL.

Chad Tracy, Red Sox: Tracy took over as manager after the Red Sox got off to a 10-17 start. He went 77-58, making the playoffs. The turnaround featured an absurd stretch during which the Red Sox won 32 of 37 games.

Will Venable, White Sox: Venable became a first-time manager for the 2025 season, taking over a team that lost a modern MLB-record 121 games the previous year. They lost 102 in 2025, but this season improved by 24 games and made the playoffs. This wasn't based much on huge free agency additions or trades for a lot of outside help. It was mostly internal improvement.

Pete Crow-Armstrong, Cubs: We'd seen flashes of the upside before, but PCA put everything together in 2026. He finished a .280/.372/.570 (156 OPS+) hitter with 31 doubles, five triples, 45 home runs, 107 RBI, 119 runs and 9.8 WAR. He led the majors in WAR, runs, home runs and led the NL in slugging percentage, OPS and OPS+. He became the seventh player ever to join the 40-40 club, too.

Shohei Ohtani, Dodgers: The four-time MVP looked like he was going to win a fifth for the first half of the season, but injuries caught up to him late. Still, at the plate, Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 26 doubles, four triples, 30 home runs, 81 RBI, 89 runs, 11 steals and 3.2 WAR. On the mound, he was 8-2 with a 1.79 ERA, 0.95 WHIP and 95 strikeouts in 85 ⅔ innings with 3.2 WAR.

Brice Turang, Brewers: Nationally underrated, Turang still hasn't made an All-Star Game, though he did start 2026 as a member of Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. In the regular season, Turang hit .268/.366/.450 (124 OPS+) with 37 doubles, three triples, 21 home runs, 100 RBI, 102 runs and 7.3 WAR, rating out as one of the best defenders in baseball.

Jacob Misiorowski, Brewers: There was upside to dream on here entering the season and it became a dream season. In 30 starts, Miz posted a 1.80 ERA, 0.80 WHIP and 252 strikeouts in 174 ⅔ innings. He went 16-5 for the team with the best record in baseball and led the majors in ERA, WHIP and strikeouts, among other things.

Chris Sale, Braves: The spindly left-hander won his first Cy Young at age 35 in 2024. He was only able to make 27 starts this season, but he was better in a few rate stats. Overall, he was 14-9 with a 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP and 200 strikeouts against only 31 walks in 162 ⅔ innings.

Cristopher Sánchez, Phillies: Early in the season, Sánchez moved to the front of the line after a scoreless streak of 50 ⅔ innings. At midseason, he started the All-Star Game in Philly. He finished the season 18-7 with a 2.91 ERA, 1.20 WHIP and 231 strikeouts in 207 innings. He led the majors in pitcher WAR at 8.1.

Carson Benge, Mets: The 2024 first-rounder made the team out of spring training and hit .282/.346/.430 with 20 home runs, 22 steals and 4.3 WAR.

Sal Stewart, Reds: It's a fight of Old School vs. New School. Stewart only posted 1.8 WAR, but he had 32 home runs and 111 RBI, putting him in rarefied air for a rookie. He's one of just 15 rookies ever with at least 30 homers and 100 RBI. The last eight players to do so won Rookie of the Year. The only ones who didn't win came before there was an award or someone else did it in the same season (two rookies in 1950 got to 30-100).

JJ Wetherholt, Cardinals: Defensive metrics love Wetherholt and help push him to 4.5 WAR in 139 games. He hit .242/.339/.365 with 17 homers, 14 steals and 89 runs.

Jhoan Duran, Phillies: In his first full season with the Phillies, Duran closed down 33 of his 35 save chances with a 1.82 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and 84 strikeouts in 59 ⅓ innings.

Mason Miller, Padres: In 70 innings across 66 appearances, Miller pitched to a 1.67 ERA, 0.90 WHIP and struck out 129 hitters. He won five games and converted 38 of his 41 save chances.

Trevor Megill, Brewers: Though the Brewers didn't always employ a traditional closer, Megill was the closest thing to it, securing 30 saves in 33 chances with a 2.63 ERA, 0.89 WHIP and 69 strikeouts in 61 2/3 innings.

Don Mattingly, Phillies: Mattingly started the season as the bench coach before taking over a 9-19 team for the fired Rob Thomson. Immediately, the Phillies got hot. They ended up going 79-55 under Mattingly, making the playoffs yet again despite starting 10 games under .500.

Pat Murphy, Brewers: Managers almost never win this award in back-to-back seasons because it's generally given to the guy whose team most exceeded expectations. How could that possibly happen two straight years? Well, Murphy now is going for three. In 2025, the Brewers set a franchise record with 97 wins and had the best record in baseball. In 2026, they set a franchise record with 103 wins and had the best record in baseball.

Walt Weiss, Braves: In 2025, the final season of Brian Snitker's career, the Braves were a disappointing 76-86. Weiss was hired in the offseason and went 94-68, getting the Braves back on top in the NL East after a two-year hiatus.

#2447. Warriors reportedly aren't paying Kristaps Porziņģis as former All-Star combats health issues

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Golden State Warriors are withholding payments to Kristaps Porziņģis on his $20 million salary as he remains away from the team, according to ESPN. Porziņģis signed a two-year, $40 million contract with the Warriors over the summer that included a $3 million guarantee for the 2027-28 season. However, to this point, he has not been able to suit up for the Warriors as he has dealt with undisclosed health problems. Porziņģis has reportedly considered stepping away from basketball altogether, but has not publicized any decisions. Porziņģis does not currently plan to challenge the Warriors on this decision, according to The Athletic.

A spokesperson for the National Basketball Players Association declined to comment when reached by CBS Sports.

Porziņģis has been dealing with health issues since the end of his tenure with the Boston Celtics. He previously disclosed a diagnosis of POTS, or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, but that diagnosis appears to be in some dispute. Warriors coach Steve Kerr said in a radio interview earlier this year that Atlanta Hawks general manager Onsi Saleh "said it's not actually POTS," but then walked back his comments a few days later.

Porziņģis has been away from the team since late September. He met with general manager Mike Dunleavy and vice president of player health and performance Rick Celebrini in mid-October; after that meeting, the Warriors announced that he would be "around the team," but that has thus far not been the case, at least publicly.

Porziņģis released the following statement on his health in October, later adding, specifically, that he does not have HIV or AIDS.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap. Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon," Porziņģis wrote. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."

NBA players are typically paid regardless of health status, but teams will occasionally withhold salary if they believe the player is in breach of contract. The most notable example occurred between Ben Simmons and the Philadelphia 76ers during the 2021-22 season, when Simmons wanted to be traded. The 76ers maintained that Simmons refused to play in regular-season games and failed to show up for the start of training camp, but Simmons cited his mental health as the reason for his limited engagement with the team. Simmons was eventually traded to the Brooklyn Nets, and he and the 76ers agreed to a settlement that saw Simmons recoup a portion of the withheld salary.

The Warriors are attempting to trade Porziņģis in an effort to utilize his $20 million cap figure. While he would not have trade value as a player given his health status, he is essentially an expiring contract with only that small $3 million guarantee on the books for next season. That could potentially make him valuable to a team looking to move off of longer-term money, or the Warriors could entice another team into a trade using draft picks with Porziņģis serving only as the matching salary.

Golden State has gotten off to a surprisingly successful 5-3 start this season despite Porziņģis' absence, thanks in large part to the stellar performance of Stephen Curry and the emergence of rookie Yaxel Lendeborg as a foundational player. On paper, Porziņģis is exactly the sort of player this roster needs: a center who can shoot 3-pointers to complement Draymond Green, a poor shooting power forward. As it grows increasingly unlikely that Porziņģis will ever suit up for Golden State again, though, a trade is the only real path the Warriors have to making the best of a bad situation.

#2445. Robinson Canó Jr., son of eight-time MLB All-Star, agrees to $1 million deal with Marlins, per reports

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Miami Marlins have reached a preliminary agreement with 16-year-old Robinson Canó Jr. that stands to make him part of the club's 2028 international signing class. The agreement is worth $1 million, reports Mike Rodriguez.

MLB rules state that an international amateur free agent player is eligible to sign with an MLB organization between Jan. 15 and Dec. 15 of his signing class year. He must turn 17 before Sept. 1 of the year in which he signs.

Canó Jr., a highly regarded shortstop out of the Dominican Republic who bats right-handed, is the son of former MLB great Robinson Canó. The elder Canó spent parts of 17 seasons in the majors, the majority of which came with the New York Yankees. Over that span, Canó earned eight All-Star selections and three Gold Gloves; racked up 2,639 hits and 335 home runs; and won a World Series ring as a member of the 2009 Yankees. He went on to sign a large free-agent contract with the Seattle Mariners, where he played from 2014-18.

Canó's career total of 68.7 WAR would under normal circumstances make him a strong candidate for election to the Baseball Hall of Fame. However, two suspensions for positive PED tests make it unlikely he'll get a plaque, at least while he's on the BBWAA ballot. He last appeared in the majors in 2022 as a member of the Atlanta Braves.

Canó Jr. is also the grandson of José Canó, who appeared in the majors with the 1989 Houston Astros, which puts him in line to be a third-generation major leaguer.

#2443. Caleb Williams, Baker Mayfield turn 'SNF' into turnover fest as Bears overcome interceptions

Caleb Williams, Baker Mayfield turn 'SNF' into turnover fest as Bears overcome interceptions originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

Through a combined 10 games this season, Baker Mayfield and Caleb Williams totaled just three interceptions.

For Williams, his limited turnovers have helped lead an elite Bears offense, emerging as a potential Super Bowl contender. Mayfield has also historically taken care of the football; despite playing through injuries in 2026, the veteran has at least been careful with his passes.

But both former Heisman Trophy winners and No. 1 overall picks had an ugly showing on "Sunday Night Football," which wound up being a game full of turnovers. Mayfield and Williams combined for six interceptions — and it led to a wacky, back-and-forth game between the Bears and Buccaneers, which Chicago narrowly escaped with a 27-24 win.

Here's a look at the collection of interceptions between Williams and Mayfield on Sunday night and how the Bears still overcame their turnovers.

MORE: Which NFL trade candidates boosted - or hurt - their stocks in Week 9?

Williams has always been a fairly accurate quarterback who rarely turns the ball over — he came into 2026 with 13 interceptions in two full seasons. Through five games, he was playing a clean brand of football, only throwing a pick in September against the Vikings.

Everything unraveled for Williams against Tampa Bay, though. With the Bears pushed back beyond the 20-yard line on a 2nd & Goal, Williams went for a shot to the end zone that wound up hurting Chicago in the second quarter.

Tykee Smith grabbed the first Williams pick of the night.

Just minutes later, after a Buccaneers turnover on downs, Williams' next throw was also an interception to Zyon McCollum.

The end of the second quarter wound up being littered with turnovers. Right after getting the ball back with a chance to add points before halftime, McCollum got him again, diving to make an interception that was awarded after a review.

The fourth Williams interception was less his fault than just an unfortunate bounce. Looking for Luther Burden in the third quarter, the pass bounced off Burden into the air, and Alex Anzalone was in the perfect spot to make the play.

It became the first four-interception game of Williams' NFL career.

MORE:4 quarterbacks who boosted their early MVP cases in Week 9

Mayfield, meanwhile, had not thrown multiple interceptions in a game since last December against the Dolphins. After not throwing a single pass against the Falcons last week, he put the ball in a bit more danger in Week 9.

Toward the end of the first half, Mayfield was looking for Tez Johnson when Cam Lewis picked him off.

The far more critical interception came in the third quarter. Mayfield, moments after Williams' fourth pick, was trying to get the ball to Cade Otton for a short gain when Jaylon Johnson jumped in front of the tight end, grabbed the ball, then got a block en route to the end zone.

The pick-six made it a two-score Bears lead, and it was the sixth interception of the game between the two teams.

For a moment, it appeared the Bears' fifth turnover of the night would be the final nail in the coffin, despite their late lead.

Reuben Bain had a huge hit on Luther Burden with under four minutes remaining that knocked the ball free, also sending the wide receiver to the locker room with an injury. The fumble was recovered by Tampa Bay, which trailed by eight.

Mayfield's clutch gene showed up in the big moment. Bucky Irving powered into the end zone for a touchdown, then Mayfield ran one in for the two-point conversion that tied it at 24 as Burden's fumble cost the Bears.

In the end, though, Williams and the Bears' offense showed up when it mattered most. Chicago drove 49 yards over eight plays, highlighted by a 38-yard pass to Colston Loveland, setting up a game-winning field goal from Cairo Santos.

Despite five turnovers, nine penalties and a blown late lead, Chicago found a way to improve to 7-2, looking more like a Super Bowl contender with every game that passes.
