#2442. NBA Panic Meter: Why Nuggets, Heat, Suns should be worried after just two weeks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We've now seen two weeks of the 2026-27 season. Is that enough time to draw conclusions? Almost certainly not. No team has even played 10% of its schedule yet, and outlier stretches are inevitable. Case in point: last year's champion, the New York Knicks, had a mostly healthy 2-9 stretch last January that included losses to the tanking Dallas Mavericks and Sacramento Kings. Weird things can happen for a few weeks.

But the first few weeks give us our first taste of who these teams are, and inevitably several will be worse than we expected. We may not have seen enough of a sample at this point to write anyone off completely, but alarm bells are starting to ring in a few notable markets. So let's go through a few of these struggling teams and figure out just how much reason there is to panic after two weeks.

It's easy to forget this now, but New York's championship season started relatively slowly. The Knicks won their first two games, but lost their next three. Mike Brown gave a lengthy and informative monologue about some of their process issues after one of those losses, a road defeat at the hands of the Milwaukee Bucks, and the Knicks righted the ship from there. And aside from that disastrous January stretch, they were mostly great.

It's hard not to look back on that stretch now, as the Knicks limp through a slow start to their title defense. Brown has echoed many of the same criticisms he made last October, most notably the offense's tendency to stand around rather than committing to the all-out motion machine that powered the greatest playoff offense of all time last spring. Perhaps that style wasn't fully replicable for this group across 82 games. That doesn't mean it can't be summoned again in April. All four Knicks losses have come by single digits. I'm going to need more than two weeks before I start worrying about Jalen Brunson's team in clutch settings. The Knicks were the fourth-most efficient late-clock shooting team in the NBA this season. They're 28th so far this season. That's going to change.

Brunson's offseason wrist surgery is a reasonable concern. His shooting is down from everywhere, even the foul line. Maybe he'll need a midseason break to get right. Mikal Bridges is (slowly) starting to make shots again. He needs to be more aggressive, and his on-ball defense has slipped. He was never going to match the intensity he played with in the postseason given his aversion to contact, but he'll have to improve on this front. Karl-Anthony Towns needs to stop fouling, but that's hardly new. Josh Hart is missing too much in the paint, but it's too early to draw conclusions there. OG Anunoby will start making 3s because he always does.

The October Knicks look like a team that spent July, August and September celebrating. If they still look like that in December, panic becomes reasonable. For now, the concerns are relatively light. They have a proven formula, and the big concern that did exist before the season -- the backup center situation -- has thus far been a relative strength. A championship earns you quite a bit more grace than the rest of these teams deserve.

If you shouldn't write off teams after two weeks, then you certainly shouldn't do so to rookies. Still, Darryn Peterson has certainly been the worst of the much-ballyhooed top four in June's draft. He's never getting to the basket or the line, not quite prerequisites for stardom at his size given his shooting, but enormously important traits for an aspiring star guard. Defense has been an adventure as well, though that's to be expected for a rookie guard, and the early returns on his fit with Keyonte George have been clunky. The Jazz ranking 29th in offense for any stretch in which they're actively trying to win is jarring. Will Hardy had the Jazz in the top five offensively in his debut 2022-23 season before the front office broke up the team at the trade deadline.

One of the motivating factors in selecting Peterson over Rookie of the Year favorite Cameron Boozer was February's acquisition of Jaren Jackson Jr., who is currently sidelined with a torn MCL. Considering his injury history in Memphis, his long-term reliability poses real concerns, yet Utah banked most of its interior defense on him, at least in the short term, when it traded Walker Kessler to the Lakers. It's hard not to wonder about an alternate timeline in which the Jazz chose Boozer and kept Kessler instead of trading for Jackson.

If we were purely talking about the 2026-27 season, the panic meter would be higher here. We're not. The Jazz wanted to be competitive this season. There's still plenty of time for that to happen, and the eventual return of Jusuf Nurkić should help on that front for a Utah team that has gotten very little out of the center position. The real championship window, even under the most optimistic projections, was always a few years down the line. The Jazz are still young and asset-rich. There's plenty of time to right the ship. Teams with more invested in this season specifically can't say the same.

The defense is bad, but the defense is always bad. They're at the bottom of the league in 3-point volume, but they're always at the bottom of the league in 3-point volume. Aaron Gordon is no longer finding easy looks at the rim nor finishing remotely effectively, but he's spent most of the last two seasons hurt, so he might simply need time to work himself back into a groove. These were predictable concerns. Nikola Jokić was supposed to paper over them like he always does.

So far this year, he hasn't. The best player of the 2020s is suddenly human, and the Nuggets are not built to win with Jokić as anything less than divine. His own defense has been perpetually shaky, but he's always at least been an elite possession-finisher. Since becoming a full-time starter in his second season, he's never had a defensive rebounding rate below 26%. He's below 22% so far this season. He's currently tying his career-high in turnovers per game, and his assists are back to single digits for the first time since 2024.

The real issues, though, are with his scoring. Jokić's overall statistical decline after a midseason knee injury last season was well documented, but what flew under the radar at the time was the precipitous decline in his 3-point shooting following a wrist injury. This was a big driver of last season's playoff upset at the hands of the Minnesota Timberwolves. Rudy Gobert didn't have to defend him out to the 3-point line, and considering Denver's shooting deficiencies elsewhere, that allowed the Wolves to completely take away the rim. Jokić is 7-of-31 from 3 so far this season. More distressingly, his legendary intermediate finishing is slipping. After five straight years in the 95th percentile or better in terms of efficiency, his runner is down to the 86th percentile, according to Synergy Sports. His hook shot, similarly dominant, is in the 50th. His free-throw attempt rate has nearly been cut in half since last season.

There's no point in talking about the defense, the shooting, or the iffy DeMar DeRozan fit if this is the case. Either Jokić is one of the best two or three players in the world or the Nuggets are not to be taken seriously as a championship contender. Jokić has earned a lot more deference than a six-game judgment. Nobody should be surprised if he's the MVP frontrunner in a month. Those other concerns will merit closer looks if he is, because even the idealized version of this roster is pretty flawed. But there's no scenario in which these Nuggets meaningfully contend if Jokić doesn't improve. For now, that's really all that matters here.

The Suns earn the dubious distinction of becoming the first team of the 2026-27 season to have their dysfunction leaked to the press. Ironically, the thing they're reportedly upset about isn't even really the problem. Chris Haynes has reported that the Suns locker room is frustrated by the roster's lack of a point guard. But Phoenix does have a point guard; it just isn't starting him. Let's compare Phoenix's offense with Collin Gillespie on the floor to how it plays without him, using stats from Cleaning the Glass.

This isn't rocket science. The Suns assist on almost 74% of their made field goals when Gillespie plays and below 60% when he doesn't. Both Devin Booker and Miles Bridges see their true shooting improve by at least eight percentage points with Gillespie on the floor. Starting Jalen Green isn't working. Whether it's in deference to his status as a No. 2 overall pick, his contract or an unfounded belief in his value, this experiment has failed. It's time to start Gillespie and add a more traditional point guard behind him.

So the point guard issues are solvable. You know what the bigger problem is? The Suns have completely lost the high-effort identity they built last season. Let's compare where the Suns ranked last year and this year in some notable areas.

Some of this comes down to bad opponents' shooting luck. Some of it is the absence of Mark Williams, because it has forced Khaman Maluach into a role he simply is not ready for (center has been perhaps Phoenix's biggest problem area). Most of it is rotational. Green isn't exactly known for playing hard or defending. Neither is Miles Bridges. Key players from last year like Jordan Goodwin, Ryan Dunn and Rasheer Fleming are playing less. The Suns simply aren't talented enough to win at the rate they did last year if they aren't playing as hard as they did then.

The Suns don't exactly have a pivot here. They don't control any of their own first-round picks in the seven-year trade window except for a 2032 selection that is currently frozen. They're not going to be able to trade Booker for a haul and reboot this thing, either. He's 30, never gets to the rim and is a declining 3-point shooter who seemingly needs to play next to the right type of playmaking point guard. His supermax contract has albatross potential. After giving up their 2033 first-round pick for Bridges, the Suns largely locked themselves into this core for the foreseeable future. There was never championship upside here, but for a team this heavily leveraged, this level of performance is simply unacceptable.

The following clip sums up one of Miami's biggest ongoing challenges:

Look at Tim Hardway here.. and then look at davion pic.twitter.com/qPTTtlY0Oq

The Heat have a reputation, and one of its pillars is defensive tenacity. Davion Mitchell obviously has that in spades. But given the unorthodox roster-building challenges of using two big men as your primary shot creators, the Heat have had to embrace players that don't. Tim Hardaway Jr. is on this roster because the Heat so badly need shooting around Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo. He is not yet making shots. He is also doing, well, this, defensively. Klay Thompson is getting hunted more mercilessly than almost any player in the NBA. The Heat have shooting. They have defense. They have alarmingly few players who offer both.

They have even fewer who can create their own shots. Antetokounmpo, Adebayo and Mitchell are the only members of the Heat who generated at least 30% of their made field goals without an assist. Toss Andrew Wiggins onto the pile, and everyone else who averages at least 10 minutes a game is assisted on 80% or more of their made shots.

Wiggins is averaging career-lows in everything. Miami's relatively egalitarian, pick-and-roll-less offense of a season ago suited him. Adjusting to the Antetokounmpo show thus far has been a struggle. Nikola Jović is veering dangerously close to dead money on their cap for the next four years. None of the core players, not Mitchell, nor Antetokounmpo, nor even Adebayo, is defending at the level expected. This was supposed to be a top-five defense. It's been in the bottom five thus far, and while some opponent shooting regression is coming, Miami's defense is designed to allow the very 3-pointers that are killing it.

Aside from simply having one of the best players in the world, it's hard to point to a distinct strength for the Heat. They're not shooting, defending or rebounding especially well. They're not winning the possession game. They're running quite a bit, but their transition offense ranks 24th in efficiency, according to Synergy Sports.

This is a team very much still finding itself, but it's one without many of the tools that made Antetokounmpo's Milwaukee teams work or the distinct advantages Miami's vaunted culture typically created for it. This roster is at least a trade or two away, but with minimal draft capital, addressing the holes here will be difficult. It might take multiple transaction cycles to get this right.

Antetokounmpo is in his 30s now and has a growing history of lower-body injuries. He might not have that many more prime seasons to waste. He's playing at a superstar level right now, and it just isn't clear how equipped Miami is to take advantage of that after giving up practically everything of value it had besides Adebayo just to get him.

#2440. Tarik Skubal contract predictions: Ace's new deal could break multiple MLB records for a pitcher

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tarik Skubal is about to become a very, very rich man. The two-time Cy Young winner and arguably the best pitcher in baseball hits free agency this winter, and it stands to reason that he'll break the record for highest-paid pitcher in MLB history, both by total value and average annual value.

By total value, Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto currently holds that record thanks to the 12-year, $325 million contract he signed ahead of the 2024 season (we're eliminating Shohei Ohtani from the running for obvious reasons, though his 10-year, $700 million deal would clearly lead the list).

As for AAV, Ohtani again tops the class at $70 million a year, but for those who only pitch, Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander share the record at $43.33 million annually.

The expectation is that Skubal will break both records, even as the owners try to tamp down on spending in the ongoing CBA negotiations. Just how high could those figures go? CBS Sports experts pulled out their calculators.

Mike Axisa: Seven years and $325.5 million. That's $46.5 million per season and it would break the records for average annual value (Max Scherzer's and Justin Verlander's $43.3 million) and total guarantee (Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million) for a pitcher. I would expect there to be an opt out because those are just the cost of doing business these days. Maybe even multiple opt outs. Scott Boras loves to break records, though, and this contract allows him to break two.

Dayn Perry: I'll say eight years, $350 million. Likewise, that sets the record for total contract value and AAV for a pitcher. Normally, I'd ding him a bit for those elbow problems in his walk year, but he was mostly dominant after returning ahead of schedule. I also think Skubal will benefit from an aggressive pre-lockout market and from a pretty thin free agent class overall.

Matt Snyder: Eight years, $400 million. This gets him the record deal for pitchers both in terms of the guarantee and the average annual value. I'm probably going too low on the years, but I feel like teams have been burned so many times before on the length of pitcher deals due to injury that this holds down the market a bit. Ever so slightly. I do think there will be opt outs after years three and five.

#2435. Why MLB could see an early free agency frenzy before the potential Dec. 1 lockout

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Most of the season, my assumption was that November would be a slow month for the hot stove. There is a new collective bargaining agreement coming, likely after a lockout, and I figured teams would not want to commit significantly to future payroll without first seeing what the new CBA would bring. Salary cap, stiffer competitive balance tax penalties, whatever.

A perfectly reasonable stance, that is, and I say that as someone who is happy to call out teams and owners who do not appear to be putting forth the best effort to contend, if you catch my drift. My assumption was November would be slow. I am here now to tell you why my assumption not just may be wrong, but likely is wrong, and the hot stove will burn bright in November.

The CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, or four weeks from Tuesday. Here now are four reasons why MLB clubs could be active between now and then.

MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents in November 2021, just before the last CBA expired and the owners locked out the players. That includes the Rangers, who spent more than $560 million on Jon Gray, Corey Seager, and Marcus Semien. Those three later helped the Rangers win the franchise's first World Series title in 2023. Five players signed nine-figure contracts in the weeks leading up to the last lockout.

It is not only the teams we must consider here. More than 140 players became free agents the day after the World Series, and you can be sure many (most?) of them would prefer to sign before the lockout. They want to get their contract locked in and know where they'll play next season so they can find a place to live, get the kids enrolled in school, etc. Peace of mind during the lockout will go a long way.

MLB's owners did not propose a salary cap during the last round of labor negotiations, but there was similar uncertainty about what the upcoming CBA would bring, and teams spent lots of money anyway. Past behavior can inform us about what to expect in the future and what we saw leading into the last lockout suggests it will be a busy four weeks.

During the last lockout, MLB amended its posting agreement with Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league and paused the 45-day negotiating window during the lockout. Seiya Suzuki was posted on Nov. 22, 2021, his 45 days were paused when the lockout began on Dec. 1, then they resumed when the lockout ended on March 10, 2022. Suzuki signed with the Cubs on March 18.

NPB players will not have the same luxury this year. MLB has declined to amend its posting agreement this offseason, according to The Athletic, so NPB players potentially face a hard Dec. 1 signing deadline even though they were officially posted on Nov. 1. They won't get the full 45 days because players cannot sign MLB contracts during the lockout. Their posting window is really 30 days.

This applies to three of our top 50 free agents: Hanshin Tigers third baseman Teruaki Sato (No. 4), Seibu Lions righty Kaima Taira (No. 19), and Hokkaido Nippon Ham Fighters righty Hiromi Itoh (No. 26). All three were posted on Nov. 1 and their 45-day posting window should run through Dec. 16. Instead, they must sign by Dec. 1 with the lockout looming, or return to Japan for 2027.

Tarik Skubal, far and away the best free agent on the market, is expected to sign before the lockout, reports ESPN. There is always a bit of a domino effect with top free agents. Several big spenders (Blue Jays, Cubs, Dodgers, Mets, etc.) are expected to pursue Skubal, and the teams that lose out could quickly pivot to their secondary targets to avoid being left empty-handed.

We saw a good example of this domino effect last offseason. The Dodgers beat out the Mets for Kyle Tucker and agreed to terms with the outfielder on Jan. 16. The Mets quickly pivoted and agreed to a contract with Bo Bichette just a few hours later. They had money to spend and a void in the lineup, and after losing out on their top target, New York quickly pivoted to Plan B.

The sooner Skubal signs, the sooner second-tier free agent starters like Freddy Peralta and Trevor Rogers will come off the board. Teams need pitching, always and forever, and once the best available starter comes off the board, there figures to be a rush to get whoever's left. Skubal is expected to sign before the lockout. Other starters won't be far behind then.

Even if the MLB Players Association relents and agrees to a salary cap, it is unlikely the cap will be fully implemented in 2027. MLB has expressed a willingness to phase in a salary cap over some number of years and, honestly, it's a must. It will be impossible for big payroll clubs like the Dodgers, Mets, and Yankees to trim payroll and get cap-compliant immediately after the lockout.

November may be the last chance for all teams, not just those with deep pockets, to spend freely and have contracts grandfathered into whatever economic system the new CBA brings. Spend now, deal with the consequences later. That kind of thing. It may sound foolish -- the bill will come due eventually, right? -- but rarely is the hot stove league and free agency rational.

"You prepare under the current system, and then you adjust along the way," Blue Jays president Mark Shapiro told Sportsnet last month. "Any new system adopted, there will be a timeframe for adjustment into that system. I don't think any new system adopted would cause for immediate action."

#2433. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2432. Mariners hire Cubs executive with no managerial experience as new manager

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After a colossally disappointing 2026 season, the Seattle Mariners are bringing in a first-time manager. The Mariners have named Chicago Cubs director of player development Jason Kanzler their new manager, the team announced Tuesday. Seattle fired manager Dan Wilson after the season.

"Our goal in this process was finding a manager with the ability to challenge all of us to improve," president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto said in a statement. "Jason has the mindset, expertise, communication skills, and intensity to help create a championship standard here in Seattle."

The Mariners will be Kanzler's first managerial job at any level. At 36, he will be the second-youngest manager in baseball, older than only 34-year-old Washington Nationals skipper Blake Butera.

Bringing in a manager with zero previous managerial experience at any level is a rare move, certainly, though it is not unprecedented. Most notably, the New York Yankees hired Aaron Boone straight from the broadcasting booth in 2018. Boone had no managerial or coaching experience at any level. He's led the Yankees to the postseason eight times in nine seasons.

"I am thrilled to join the Mariners organization and I'm looking forward to hitting the ground running," Kanzler said in a statement. "This team has an immense amount of talent in all facets of the game, and my coaching staff and I are excited to access and unlock this team's full potential."

Kanzler may have no prior managerial experience, but this will not be his first time on a big-league staff. He was a major-league coach with the Houston Astros in 2022 and their assistant hitting coach in 2023, and had coached in their farm system previously. The Cubs hired Kanzler to oversee their player development in 2024.

Former Astros manager Joe Espada was reportedly the other finalist for the Mariners job.

The Mariners went 76-86 this past season and finished five games back in the woebegone AL West. A year ago, they went to Game 7 of the ALCS and were five outs away from their first-ever trip to the World Series. Seattle entered 2026 as a trendy World Series pick and instead fell flat, mostly because so many core hitters underperformed.

Kanzler will be the team's third manager since Dipoto was hired to run baseball operations in September 2015, joining Scott Servais (2015-24) and Wilson (2024-26).

#2430. Pröschtli! Swiss Devils Lead the Way for Connor Hellebuyck’s 4-0 Shutout of Maple Leafs

For weeks, we've been watching as several Devils have been doing the little things that help win hockey games. Connor Brown has become a mongoose around the net, mixing it up with energy in close and being rewarded with goals. Cody Glass has been forechecking like a machine, forcing opposing defenders to move faster and causing turnovers that lead to Devils chances. Even Jack Hughes, the Devils' most dangerous scoring threat, has been backchecking like his life depends on it. All over the ice, the Devils are doing things that don't necessarily end up on the scoresheet, but are some of the most critical things that contribute to wins.

Since the beginning of the season, the poster child for this kind of hockey has been Timo Meier. Timo has been using his big frame to cause havoc in front of opposing goalies, gotten his stick in passing lanes above the dots in the defensive zone, and taking the body on forwards in the neutral zone. That said, Timo has caught some flack this season for not getting on the scoresheet like some believe he should. He's been firing away, but despite playing some damn good hockey, just hasn't lit the lamp yet. Tonight, that changed.

Timo busted out tonight, potting two goals to go along with goals by Nico and the utility knife, Connor Brown. If he can use this game as a launching pad to start racking up goals while still playing a complete game like he has been, he will be a real… Swiss army knife.

The game started relatively slowly with neither team registering a shot on goal through the first four minutes of play. Even almost 14 minutes into the game, each team had only taken three shots on the opposing netminder. For their part, the Devils' shots to this point had largely been kept to outside the faceoff dots, with Anthony Stolarz handling the long-range pucks with relative ease. Same in the Devils' end, where most shots came from the point, and Hellebuyck kicked out most rubber with little drama.

Aside from a few weird bounces that led to shots in close at funky angles, everything was pretty even-keel throughout the opening period. Just a quiet beginning to the game.

The Devils outshot the Leafs 7-4 in the first, but both teams go scoreless. We go into the locker room knotted at 0.

The second period began much faster than the first, with the Devils looking particularly energetic. I mention it in a little more detail below, but Jesper Bratt had a strong move to the net that started from the right point. When a player can start his drive to the net from where some players tee-up point shots, you know he has a strong stride. In any event, Bratt's move inside was saved.

Off an offensive zone draw to Stolarz's right, Nico wins the puck back to Declan Chisholm who sends a dart across toward the center of the ice. While the scrum at the dot was going on (including the Leafs' McCabe and Nylander running into one another), Timo Meier quietly drifted toward the middle of the ice, between the hash marks. Chisholm's dart made its way through some players to Meier who took one of the most "this-puck-better-go-into-the-back-of-the-frigging-net" follow-throughs I've ever seen. Timo absolutely unloaded on Chisholm's pass, and it did indeed find the back of the net. Timo's heating up! 1-0, Devils!

After the goal, the Devils started firing from everywhere, trying to test Stolarz. Timo started feeling it, shooting from outside the dot. Evan Rodrigues took a shot from just about on the boards. Just rubber flying from everywhere. I really liked seeing this; old Devils teams would sit back and grip their sticks a bit harder after getting a lead. This team seems to smell blood in the water when they get a lead.

This approach paid off at the 12:44 mark, when Jack Hughes took a drop pass from Jesper Bratt between the circles and made a quick move to the center of the ice where he took a quick, heavy shot on goal. Timo Meier, he of the big body, was camped in front of the net and managed to get a stick on Jack's shot, deflecting it upward and into the net. After having only scored one goal to this point in the season, Timo is on the scoresheet with two! Devils lead, 2-0!

Although I've been talking up Timo in this recap, the latter minutes of the second period really went to Connor Hellebuyck, who did well to keep rebounds wide and kick the puck out when there was any danger. He only faced a handful of shots through two periods, but none of that handful felt truly dangerous. To this point in the game, Connor and Timo have the Devils looking firmly in control. Everyone goes into the intermission to get orange slices with the Devils up 2-0.

Early in the third period, Jack Hughes snuck in behind the Toronto defense to collect a bouncing home-run pass and get a breakaway on Stolarz, who made an excellent glove save on Jack's shot.

A few minutes later, Jack shows how much his game has grown in the last year. Of course, we expect him to get those breakaways and give fits to opposing goalies. Tonight, just after the five-minute mark in the third period while the Devils were on a power play, the Leafs had the opportunity to break up ice for a shorthanded try. Except there was one Devil back to responsibly cover for his defenders… Jack Hughes. I absolutely love seeing this from Jack. Although Toronto got the shot off, it was easily handled by Hellebuyck. Just a huge, responsible play by someone we're seeing mature into a complete player.

Around the eight-minute mark, Hellebuyck makes one of his best saves of the night, robbing Auston Matthews with a quick glove. If Matthews scores there, it changes the entire complexion of the game. Instead, just over a minute later, Nico Hischier buries a rebound on a post-toe-drag shot by Jack Hughes to put the game out of reach. The Swiss-trick makes it 3-0, Devils!

To close out the game, Cody Glass absolutely outhustled Gavin McKenna to get to a loose puck along the boards, which he then dished to Connor Brown at the center of the ice. Brown made no mistake from long distance, burying the dagger for the final goal of the game. Brown will be on the scoresheet, but that goal was all Cody Glass and his hustle. Regardless, 4-0, Devils! Game!

Another two points for the Devils, and Connor Hellebuyck gets his first shutout in a Devils sweater.Helle yes! Let's keep it rolling!

In my preview for this game, I wrote that one of the things that Connor Hellebuyck seems to bring to the Devils is a measure of confidence. Since he arrived in New Jersey, it looks to me like the Devils play with a bit more enthusiasm than they do in front of Jake Allen. This is not to say that Jake Allen is a bad goalie. As I noted in my preview, he's served admirably in New Jersey. It's just that Hellebuyck's goaltending style seems so calm and measured, and that poise rubs off on his teammates in front of him.

Having played goal, I know how hard it can be to find the balance between cutting the angle on a shooter and being cognizant of players on your periphery that could score easily on a rebound. Goalies are in a constant state of trying to reduce the amount of net a shooter can see while also accounting for other potential threats. Hellebuyck's movements in net are minimized because has mastered this balance. I can't think of another goalie in recent memory that effectively plays the geometry of the position as well as he does.

This is where I think his effectiveness, and in turn his teammates' confidence, comes from. He plays his angles perfectly and has fantastic rebound control. Because he doesn't need to worry about easy rebounds falling to opponents, he can be more aggressive at the top of his crease and take away huge parts of the net for his opponents to shoot at. Because of that, he doesn't need to move much to make saves.

Someone in the comments said that Hellebuyck makes difficult saves look easy by barely moving when he makes them. That's the mark of a great goaltender. We already knew he was special, but now that I see him up close in the red and black, I think he has taken the Devils to another level.

I don't want to spend too much time stating the obvious, but Jesper Bratt's rush to the outside with his power move to the net during the second period showed the kind of jets he has. Jack gets most of the praise for his skill and speed, but I firmly believe that Bratt is nearly at his level.

Much like Timo, Bratt has caught some criticism about not scoring like he should (and passing much more often than he should), but even during a "slow" start to the season, his speed and stick-handling have him toward the top of the Devils roster in terms of points. It seems like only a matter of time before he breaks out as well.

And if the Devils can get simultaneous and consistent scoring from Jack, Nico, Timo, and Bratt… I'd take them against any team in the league.

Nothing profound here. I'm just really enjoying a sustained stretch of Devils hockey for the first time in what seems like a long time. It rules.

This is an inclusion from Chris: I really love these old-school style photos. Credit to Mark Blinch for a great photograph of Timo Meier and Oliver Ekman-Larsson. There were a few more shot in this style during the game, but this is probably the best action photo that Blinch got with it.

#2424. MLB CBA negotiations timeline: League proposes delaying salary cap for 'smoother transition'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally important to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a new collective bargaining agreement.

The collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years. It covers things as mundane as players' meal allowances and travel protocols and as vital as minimum salaries, the structure of free agency, revenue-sharing specifics, and roster sizes. Every CBA can be distilled down to a fight over money, or, more specifically, how the league's revenues will be divided between players and team owners.

The first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history. That was the handiwork of Marvin Miller, the pioneering head of the Players Association (i.e., the players union) and belated Hall of Famer. It was Miller's organizing skills, foresight, and training as a union economist that allowed him to make the Players Association a viable and effective labor organization. Every CBA negotiation from 1972 through 1994-95 resulted in some form and scale of labor stoppage, whether a players' strike or an owner-implemented lockout. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series because of the worst labor stoppage in the sport's history, a long run of peace followed. That peace lasted until the prior CBA negotiations, which resulted in a 99-day lockout forced by team owners and delayed the start of the 2022 season.

The current CBA negotiations have been underway for some time, and not surprisingly, the two sides remain far apart on several key issues. The biggest fight will be over the owners' renewed desire to implement a salary cap, which the union continues to view as a non-starter. The push for a cap has less to do with the notions of competitive balance and more to do with the ownership's internal belief that being the only non-salary-capped league among the major North American sports is harming franchise values. The cap, though, is but one of many pressing issues on which players and owners must find congruity.

Moving forward, the process will be uncertain and rife with posturing and pointed public comments from both sides. The hope, though, is that a new CBA will be agreed to before the middle of March 2027, at which point there's a high risk of having the 2027 season delayed or even abbreviated.

To keep you informed of the twists and turns along the way to a new CBA, we've provided a detailed timeline of negotiations. That timeline will illuminate the important and finer points of the talks and, along the way, explain the implications of the various proposals coming from each side. The hope, of course, is that all of it culminates in a timely agreement that permits a fully intact and on-time 2027 season.

To allow for a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system, MLB proposed delaying its implementation until 2028. That would give teams time to prepare and get their payrolls in order, and allow for a full offseason heading into the system. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system."

MLB also upped its salary cap/floor proposal to $258.3 million and $180.2 million, respectively. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor. It says it is willing to discuss further phase-in scenarios for a salary cap/floor system.

In its latest proposal, MLB proposed reducing the regular season from 162 games to 154 games, and adding a standard off day to every week. The league also proposed extending the Division Series from a best-of-five to a best-of-seven, and allowing higher seeded teams to select their opponents in the Wild Card Series and Division Series. As with every MLB proposal to date, the 154-game schedule and changes to the postseason format are contingent on the MLBPA accepting a salary car/floor system.

If labor strife lops off 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the consequences could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the forthcoming lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That's significant because commissioner Rob Manfred hopes to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. As such, this is a heavy incentive, at least on the league side, to not let any labor stoppage drag into June.

A poll of current MLB players across the full spectrum of salaries and service time conducted by ESPN showed strong resistance to the payroll cap and floor being demanded by ownership and league and being put forth as a precondition to every proposed change from that side. An excerpt:

How open are you to a salary cap?NL starting pitcher entering arbitration: Not open.

NL infielder making eight figures annually: Zero. No chance.

NL infielder on two-year contract: Zero. Absolute zero.

NL pre-arbitration journeyman: From what I've been told, I don't think it's good for the game. I just don't know if I know all the pros and cons of it. But, from everything we've been told, it doesn't sound like it's a good thing.

NL reliever on multiyear contract: With the right criteria, I'd be open to it.

AL starting pitcher in arbitration: I don't want it. In '94, they canceled the World Series, so if those guys can miss over half a year and miss the World Series, I think we're fully prepared to hold out for sure.

AL catcher entering arbitration: I need more information, but perhaps I would listen on it.

That's mostly strong sentiment that aligns with the MLBPA position on the cap, but it's not ironclad. MLB in negotiations and its public statements is seeking to tap into any existing divide between, broadly speaking, lower-salaried players with not much service time and more tenured veterans in their higher-earning years. There is a bit of a schism there, but it would take a substantial one to shift, in any exploitable way, the union's long-standing opposition to a cap-and-floor system. The ESPN piece covers an array of CBA topics. With the two questions related to the proposed cap, the responses can be broken down as 16 in mostly firm opposition to a cap and five not necessarily in favor but open to further discussions and reflection.

MLB proposed a series of changes to current roster rules that, in a statement, the league says are aimed at "creating more stability in rosters, getting the best players to the Major Leagues more quickly, and accelerating the pace of the offseason." Among the rule changes included in MLB's proposal are:

All the proposed roster rule changes are contingent on the MLB Players Association agreeing to a salary cap-and-floor system.

During a negotiating session with the league, the players' union puts forth its own proposed changes to the MLB Draft -- changes that are, in essence, a rejoinder to the drastic overhaul earlier put forward by MLB. Among the changes the MLBPA proposes are:

Additionally, the union proposes increasing the money payable to draftees under the incentive bonus plan and eliminating, according to the MLBPA, "the current practice of clubs deducting certain bonuses from players' continuing education benefits."

The timing of the draft has actually been a concern for front offices for years, since it was shifted later in the calendar to coincide with the All-Star break in 2021. Holding the draft in July crams both that and the trade deadline into just a few weeks and making it more difficult to allocate resources.

Commissioner Rob Manfred and interim union head Bruce Meyer each hold press conferences on the day of the All-Star Game in Philadelphia. "I think that I have an ownership group that is more united than any group in my entire time of baseball," Manfred says, referring at least obliquely to the league's push for a salary cap. "They are a group that believes in what I am arguing for."

"The supposed stewards of the game have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to convince those same fans that they don't have hope or they shouldn't have hope or that the product that they're paying to consume in record numbers is somehow broken," Meyer says of MLB's efforts to highlight perceived competitive-balance issues in the face of increasing attendance and television ratings. "I think it's perverse."

The MLBPA puts forth multiple proposals, many of them dealing with procedural matters for purposes of player health, safety, and wellness. They include:

The union's latest proposal is a reminder of the breadth of CBA discussions. Most issues are not the big-ticket items like a salary cap or lack thereof or revenue sharing structure but instead are somewhat esoteric matters that strike most fans as mundane. To players and teams, though, they're important considerations and in some instances may even provide a foundation of common ground moving forward.

More face-to-face negotiations take place, and MLB proposes more changes to the free-agency system, among other asks. MLB's latest proposal includes the following, all of which depend upon the union's acceptance of a payroll cap:

MLB in a prior proposal called for a cap on team payrolls of $245.3 million starting in 2027 and a payroll floor of $171.2 million. The league issues a statement that reads in full:

"The biggest issue baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title. Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50.

"Today, in addition to proposing the largest ever increase in the minimum salary, earned by over half of MLB players, we accepted two landmark changes to free agency that have been in place for 50 years. We agreed to both the MLBPA's proposal to provide earlier access to free agency, and their proposal to eliminate the qualifying offer system, a provision players view as a drag on free agency. We also proposed to eliminate deferred compensation and to create a new 'Cornerstone Player' provision similar to the NBA's 'Bird Rights' to give every team a fair shot at retaining their fans' favorite star players.

"We will continue working with the MLBPA during the bargaining process to improve the game for teams, players and fans."

"After making a series of proposals to reduce player compensation by billions of dollars, eliminate fundamental rights with a salary cap, and destroy the amateur entry process, Major League Baseball and team owners are now attempting to distract from the true impact their plan would have on baseball. These misleading offers are designed to look like 'improvements' but are of little or no value, given they are expressly conditioned on agreement to the league's cap system which eliminates the free market, and ensures gains for one player only come at the expense of another.

"The league also introduced a litany of additional restrictions on player rights — limiting salaries, contract length, performance, award, and signing bonuses. While MLB claims to be acting in the interest of fans, their proposals thus far are entirely consistent with owners' long-held goals: suppressing player salaries and maximizing club profits.

"Owners' attempts to pit players against players are nothing new, but they've failed in the past and will fail again now, because PA members remain unified. We are committed to achieving a fair deal that protects the rights of all players, promotes competition, and leaves our game better for future generations."

Lacking from the league's latest proposal, at least on the public-facing side, is any revisiting of the recent changes to the draft and any mention of prior proposed changes to the league's revenue-sharing system.

During these same face-to-face sessions, the MLBPA proposes a ban on prop bets placed on individual players, ESPN reports. The idea is to preempt harrassment of players by gamblers. The proposed ban would extend to bets placed on individual player performance prior to and during any MLB game. The MLBPA also requested that players be permitted to engage in paid endorsements and sponsorships with sportsbooks and prediction markets.

MLB and the MLBPA meet for face-to-face negotiations, and owners propose sweeping changes to the draft and also push for an international draft. As for the MLB Draft, formally known as the First-Year Player Draft, MLB pushes for the following changes:

"Over the last several years, college baseball has undergone a remarkable transformation," MLB says in a statement. "Expanded scholarships, NIL opportunities, revenue sharing and significant investments in facilities and player development have made college baseball an increasingly important pathway that is producing major league-ready talent at an accelerated rate. Today's top programs provide players with resources, competition and national exposure that were unimaginable a decade ago. Our proposal is designed to build on that momentum to benefit the game at the college, minor-league and major-league levels. By creating a draft system centered around college-aged players and making most college players eligible one year earlier, more players will benefit from both a college education and an elite development environment while reaching professional baseball -- and ultimately the major leagues -- more quickly. We believe these changes will strengthen college baseball and deepen fans' connection to the next generation of major league stars. We look forward to working with the MLBPA throughout the bargaining process to modernize the domestic amateur system in a way that benefits players, clubs, and fans."

As for the international draft, MLB proposed making players outside of the U.S., Puerto Rico, and Canada (who are already included in the standard draft) subject to a similar system. The international draft would, as with the proposed changes to the MLB Draft, come with a $200 million bonus cap. At present, international amateurs may sign with any team under the international free agent system, although teams do have hard budget caps each year.

The MLBPA also issues a statement in response to MLB's proposals:

Today, MLB made another set of proposals that are flat out bad for baseball, ones that would cripple the next generation of players and damage the future of our game. They would, among other things:

Players remain committed to bargaining in good faith and leaving baseball better than they found it -- the league's proposals fall woefully short.

U.S. President Donald J. Trump publicly supports MLB's efforts to implement a salary cap. "If you don't have a salary cap, you don't have a sport, because they can't help themselves," Trump says. "Football has a salary cap. They should have done it a long time ago.

"It's shocking, frankly, that they didn't put a cap on many years ago," he said, possibly referencing the 1994-95 strike. "They had a chance to do a cap, but they blew it."

Speaking to reporters following the owners' quarterly meetings, Manfred addresses the luxury-tax system he and the owners seek to replace with a cap. "We have tried mightily over several rounds of bargaining to use a competitive balance (luxury) tax to address competitive concerns," Manfred says. "And sometimes you've got to admit you failed.

"We made a proposal on one set of topics. At the outset of negotiations, I went and said myself, 'We're open to whatever ideas people have, but we need a realistic framework that addresses the fans' concerns about competitive balance.' You just can't ignore that financial penalties have not gotten it done for us."

In a call with reporters, MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer addresses the owners' proposals. "Using MLB's definition of revenue and player share as set forth in their proposal and their presentation to us, player share under their proposal would go down," Meyer says. "Player share for this season, 2026, is projected to be well over 50 percent, using, again MLB's definitions of revenues and what counts against player share.

"Had MLB's proposal been in place in 2026, players, we estimate, would lose over half a billion dollars."

Meyer also refers to a salary cap as "a form of institutionalized collusion."

"Our salary cap-and-floor proposal addresses our fans' concerns by leveling the playing field while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50-50 like the other leagues," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin responded on behalf of the league. "Under our proposal, major-league players will receive more compensation in year one of the system than in 2026. We are ready to listen if the MLBPA wants to counter our proposal at the bargaining table."

MLB and the owners publicly announce their first formal CBA proposal. Chiefly, they propose:

Using competitive balance tax (CBT), or luxury tax, payrolls as a guide, since they include benefits expenses, nine teams at present would be above the proposed cap line, while 12 teams would be below the floor. However, as Craig Goldstein points out, the amount needed to get all these teams below or above the relevant payroll thresholds amounts to an $18.7 million loss in aggregate player salary overall. Another sticking point will be how league revenues are defined. Owners no doubt seek to carve out things like real estate developments surrounding ballparks and ownership stakes in regional sports. As well, MLB's working definition of league revenues includes many expense deductions.

On another level, the fact that Manfred is able to persuade large-market, high-revenue clubs to agree to equal sharing of all local revenues is a notable development. However, such a concession by those large-market clubs may be contingent upon the implementation of a cap.

Another sticking point is that the league proposes an escrow system, as is used in the NBA and the NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld. If revenues fall short of projections, some of that money in escrow goes back to the league. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA opposes the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries.

The MLBPA makes an opening suite of proposals to the league, including:

"Today, the MLBPA (Major League Baseball Players Association) presented a comprehensive set of economic proposals designed to advance the rights and benefits of players at all levels," Meyer says in a statement released by the union. "Our goal is to preserve and improve baseball's market system, rewarding competition on and off the field. Additionally, the players' proposals provide increased revenue sharing initially guaranteeing every small market club a minimum of $240m in revenue every season. This enhanced revenue sharing includes added protections to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering. Ultimately, our proposals are designed to build upon the incredible momentum and popularity of our sport world-wide."

"We appreciate the union making a set of proposals and we look forward to continuing the bargaining process and working towards solving the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us needs to be addressed," Caplin says in a statement. "We understand their proposals are designed to benefit players. Unfortunately, they do not address and in fact exacerbate the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us we must address. The MLBPA's proposal would reduce the amount transferred to lower-revenue Clubs, weaken the Competitive Balance Tax, and lead to even more payroll disparity than exists today. For example, under the Union's proposal, the Dodgers would pay less in luxury tax payments, giving them an additional $70 million to spend on payroll."

Negotiations on a new CBA formally begin between teams and players. Among the key issues to be discussed will be the league's desire for a salary cap, drastic changes to the revenue sharing system, league expansion, possible further playoff expansion, and an international draft.

The 2022-26 Basic Agreement is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET, at which point owners are expected to lock out the players in the absence of a new agreement.

#2420. Should the NBA shorten games to 40 minutes? Pros and cons of move as league battles early season injury crisis

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Opinions vary on the causes and potential solutions for the NBA's early-season injury crisis, and an idea commissioner Adam Silver once floated is back in the conversation. Sports Illustrated's Chris Mannix said on the Open Floor podcast that he has heard that Silver likes the idea of shortening NBA games to 40 minutes. This is an idea that Silver has previously supported publicly.

"As we get more involved in global basketball, the NBA is the only league that plays 48 minutes. And I would be -- I am -- a fan of four 10-minute quarters," Silver said on The Dan Patrick Show in 2025. "I'm not sure that many others are. Putting aside what it means for records and things like that, yeah, I think that a two-hour format for a game is more consistent with modern television habits."

Silver is not the only major supporter of the idea. Mark Cuban has vouched for it as well, and given the sheer number of notable injuries the NBA has endured so far this season, the league is suddenly in a position in which it probably needs to consider pretty drastic changes to keep its best players on the floor. Is the idea of a 40-minute NBA game feasible? What are the pros and cons here, and why do the negatives ultimately outweigh the positives? Let's dive in.

Some basic math: 82 48-minute games equals 3,936 minutes of regular-season basketball for every team, before overtime. Trim games to 40 minutes and teams instead play 3,280 regular-season minutes per year, or around 17% less total basketball. Fewer minutes means fewer opportunities for players to get hurt.

That much is essentially indisputable. Where things get more promising is in the theoretical, compounding effect of playing less. If players are likelier to get hurt when they're overworked, reducing their workloads could potentially limit those more vulnerable minutes late in games and seasons because they simply aren't accumulating the same degree of wear and tear.

Fresher players would hopefully be healthier players.

College basketball games are 40 minutes. WNBA games are 40 minutes. FIBA games are 40 minutes. The NBA is the outlier here. It is the only major basketball league in which games have those eight extra minutes, and standardizing games across the sport could make it easier to translate player production across leagues.

This isn't strictly a basketball phenomenon, either. Major League Baseball is in the middle of a renaissance sparked in part by game-shortening measures like the pitch clock. Silver acknowledged this in that Dan Patrick Show interview, calling a two-hour game "more consistent with modern television habits." It's simply easier to hold the attention span of a television audience for a 40-minute game than a 48-minute game.

This has certainly been less true in the "eight champions in eight years" era we are currently living through, but the NBA tends to be more predictable than other sports when it comes to playoff outcomes. The NFL's single-elimination format makes the best teams extremely vulnerable in the postseason, and baseball is so inherently volatile because pitcher performance makes upsets so common.

Over a seven-game sample, the better team usually wins out in an NBA playoff series. This isn't absolute, of course, especially with health and 3-point variance factored in, but Cinderella runs are relatively rare in basketball. Only two NBA champions were seeded lower than No. 3 in their conference, and neither came this century. Nearly twice as many No. 1 seeds (53) have won titles than all other seeds combined (27).

Smaller samples create more volatility. It's easier for an inferior team to overcome a superior one across 40 minutes than it is across 48. Every hot shooting stretch means more; every key player in foul trouble has to miss a larger portion of the game. If you view the NBA through a purely competitive lens, this is a negative. If you view the NBA primarily as an entertainment product, creating more upsets is a real benefit of shortening games.

NBA games may last 48 minutes, but nobody actually plays anywhere near that much anymore. In fact, nobody even averages 40 minutes per game anymore, with Jamal Murray leading the league at 38.4 minutes per game thus far this season. What this essentially means is that teams could largely maintain the workloads of their superstars in a 40-minute game and simply use their bench players less.

This is the immediate reason that a change like this isn't feasible. Why on Earth would the NBA Players Association go along with a change that trivializes the majority of its membership? Stars would suddenly be more valuable than ever because they'd be playing a greater proportion of the game, but everyone else becomes less valuable for the same reason.

This has enormous team-building implications as well. Suddenly, superteams would be back in vogue because tying all of your money and assets into two or three players would make more sense in a world where fewer players are needed to get through a game or season.

On this note, it's not even clear what sort of health benefits this change would actually create. Bench players would certainly stay healthier just for playing less... but would stars benefit from this at all? That's less clear, and the NBA is obviously far more invested in keeping the best players on the court than role players.

There are theoretical fixes here, but none are perfect. The NBA could put a minutes cap on individual players, but remember, stoppages aren't uniform. Say the league sets a 30-minute cap, and a player crosses that threshold because no timeout, foul or dead-ball turnover stops the game for him to leave. How does the league handle that? It could mandate that players sit one full quarter, but doing so would inevitably lead to star players essentially playing at least one full half.

There's no clean solution to this problem, and until someone finds one, it's hard to believe this sort of change is feasible.

The length of games is only a small component of what makes the NBA schedule so grueling. Shortening games to 40 minutes wouldn't eliminate the need to travel to 41 regular-season road games. It wouldn't remove back-to-backs from the slate either, and it wouldn't bake more time into the schedule for practice, conditioning or a longer training camp.

NBA basketball is simply more difficult to play today than it was in the past. Players are more skilled and athletic than they used to be, forcing them to cover more space, play faster and endure more punishment than they once did. Shortening the game wouldn't change how it is played.

That's the danger of any incremental solution. Shortening games would carry substantial costs to the NBA. Shorter games would mean fewer commercial breaks for the television product. If the league tries it and it doesn't work, it has sacrificed revenue for nothing and is therefore less likely to take bigger financial risks to reap more substantial rewards, such as cutting games from the schedule.

Even if records and statistics aren't that important in the grand scheme of things, they're treated as sacred components of league history by many fans. Even if every other major rule has been subject to change across eras, the length of the game has been stable. That makes comparing stats and records across history at least somewhat viable. That changes if you shorten the game. Modern records become nearly unbreakable.

If the league were willing to tamper with its history in this way, there are simply lower-risk changes it could make instead of shortening games. One concept: increasing the value of 3-pointers to four points and similarly pushing 2s up to three. Doing this would narrow the value gap between shots behind the arc and those inside it, thereby incentivizing players to take more mid-range shots and, theoretically, forcing defenders to cover less ground than they do currently. One reason a change like this is unlikely is that it would make comparing numbers across eras pointless.

The NBA may one day decide it's willing to break that glass, but it has given no indication that it is prepared to do so now.

#2419. MLB proposes delaying salary cap in new negotiations as Dec. 1 CBA expiration inches nearer

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball has proposed delaying the implementation of a salary cap/floor system until 2028 as part of its latest collective bargaining agreement proposal, the league announced Tuesday. MLB says the delay is intended to provide a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system and give teams more time to prepare and get their payrolls in order.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits, including earlier free agency, a $1 million minimum salary, a 30% increase to the pre-arbitration bonus pool, and transactional reform that will reduce roster churn."

The league also newly proposed a $180.2 million salary floor and a $258.2 million salary cap. Those numbers are up from $171.2 million and $245.3 million, respectively, in the league's previous proposal in June. The $1 million minimum salary would only apply to players with at least two years of service time. The minimum salary would be $900,000 for all other players.

Four teams currently have more than $258.2 million on the books for 2027 (including arbitration projections) and 20 teams have less than $180.2 million on the books, according to FanGraphs' calculations. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027 before the transition to a salary cap/floor system in 2028.

The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the owners are expected to lock out the players at that time. The previous lockout ended on March 10, then there was a three-week spring training leading up to Opening Day. If there is a similarly lengthy lockout, it would be impossible for clubs to become salary cap-compliant in such a short period of time.

The MLB Players Association has repeatedly insisted it will not accept a salary cap/floor system, and has instead proposed a revised revenue sharing system that would funnel more money from big-market teams to small-market teams. In a statement following the league's proposal on Tuesday, the MLBPA accused owners of continuing to "propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values." The union also said that even with a delayed implementation, the league's proposal of a salary cap maintains the same "negative impacts," including a "massive reduction in player compensation" and the "elimination of fundamental player rights, including guaranteed contracts."

MLB says its push for a salary cap/floor system is intended to improve competitive balance. The small-market Milwaukee Brewers defeated the small-market Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series last week and swept big-market teams (Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees) en route to the Fall Classic.

#2416. Victor Wembanyama after historic 52-point, 24-rebound night: 'It should be more like this, more often'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Victor Wembanyama came into the 2026-27 season with expectations of taking over the title of Best in the World, but a dismal performance on opening night in a loss to the Thunder raised questions about whether we might see the Spurs' star plateau in his fourth year.

Those concerns were short-lived, as the Spurs have ripped off six straight wins after their 0-2 start. Wembanyama did his part on Wednesday night when he put together a historic stat line in a win over the Mavs, scoring 52 points, pulling down 24 rebounds and blocking eight shots in a 112-111 win.

CAREER NIGHT FOR VICTOR WEMBANYAMA 🚨🤯 52 PTS (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 24 REB (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 8 BLKFIRST PLAYER WITH 50+ PTS, 20+ REB, 5+ BLK SINCE BOB MCADOO IN 1974. pic.twitter.com/lHzUhYYSTz

It was a career-best performance for Wembanyama, who spoke after the game about finally starting to feel like he had his legs under him again after beginning the year battling an illness.

"I haven't been feeling great lately," Wembanyama said, via the Associated Press. "I've been sick for a while and today I felt like I got my legs back. So it should be more like this, more often."

While he's not going to average 52/24/8, an otherworldly stat line is what we've come to expect from the Frenchman, and he's starting to post those kinds of sensational performances more often. It's his third game in the last four with at least 36 points and his fourth game this season with five or more blocks.

For as great as he was against Dallas, Wembanyama still sees plenty of room for improvement. He highlighted his struggles shooting the ball, noting that it forces him to play a style that's less sustainable over the long haul of the regular season.

"I can still do more," Wembanyama said. "I mean, my shots weren't falling tonight and that forces me into a style of play that is exhausting. I can do it. I mean, the proof is here. I can do it, but I can be much better if my shots fall. I know it's just a matter of time."

Wembanyama has been pretty awful shooting the ball this season, hitting 24% of his threes and is just 11 of 36 from the mid-range this year. Perhaps getting his legs under him better and feeling more like himself can unlock his perimeter game, which would make him all the more terrifying.

That said, there's something encouraging for the Spurs about Wembanyama struggling to shoot and just finding a way to dominate anyway. One of the frustrations of watching the gigantic Frenchman is how he sometimes seems to forget he can basically get free buckets when he gets himself near the rim. While it's understandable that he'd want to conserve some energy in the regular season, noting it's "exhausting" to fight through defenders to get to the rim, it's what makes the Spurs the best version of themselves and that's going to be the mindset he needs in the postseason.

If he does get the jumper working, it'll lighten that load some and make the Spurs even more dynamic, but Wembanyama can't forget that his most dominant performances come when he's relentless in attacking the basket. If he can find the right balance, perhaps his proclamation that "it should be more like this, more often" can come true, and he can ascend to that Best in the World title as expected.
